Hon. E. M. MACDONOLD (Pictou), (Acting Minister of National Defence) moved that the House go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, (1) That it is expedient to amend the provisions of the Militia Pension Act by providing that the period of service entitling officers, retired compulsorily, to pension, shall be twenty years* and that any officer so retired, who served on active service during the Great War and was appointed to the Force on or after the 1st January, 1919, and prior to 31st December, 1921, and since such appointment has served continuously in the Force for not less than ten years, shall be entitled to pension as provided in section four of the said Act.
(2) That the period of service required of every militiaman to entitle him to pension shall be twenty years, or fifteen years if incapacitated for duty by infirmity of mind or body, and he shall be subject to return to service if he ceases to be incapacitated, and if he has completed fifteen but less than twenty years service, his pension shall be an annual sum equal to one-fiftieth of his annual pay and allowances for every completed year of service.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been informed of the subject matter of the resolution, has given his consent thereto and commends it to the consideration of the House.
Would the minister take this occasion to let us know the exact effect of the resolution, for purposes of discussion?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I have not my memorandum by me, but in a general

way I might explain that the original provisions of the Militia Pension Act stipulated that the period of service entitling them to pensions of both officers and men should be twenty years. In 1919, the period was reduced to ten years. It is now proposed to return to the former standard and provide that the service shall be twenty years. It has been found, particularly among non-commissioned officers and men, that many persons have been taking advantage of the shorter period to leave the service in order to secure the pension. I shall be prepared to deal with the matter fully when the resolution is in committee.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg to ask leave, under Rule 39, to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance. The matter which I wish to discuss is the case of a body of Scottish immigrants, recently landed in Canada with the assistance of the Department of Immigration, a large part of whom, to the number of about two hundred, is still camped in a disused school building near the city of Red Deer, Alberta, unable apparently to find an opportunity either to go upon the land or to secure employment. This is a situation in which departmental responsibility is involved is at once a hardship to these people themselves, and is a deterrent to future immigration into this country.
And leave having been granted:

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hous? will remember that some time ago a comparatively large party of Scottish immigrants from the Hebridean islands, to the number of between four and five hundred, came to this country. Their advent was advertised extensively throughout the Dominion and, I presume, throughout a good part of the world because the news went through at least the United States and Great Brit-
[Mr. J. H. ICine.)
ain. Those people are, I imagine, amongst the most desirable class of immigrants which this country can secure. They were accustomed to hard work; they were industrious, frugal, ambitious, anxious to succeed. They sold their little holdings in these islands and came to Canada. I had an opportunity of meeting a part of that body of men and women as they went through this city on their way to the West, and I can assure you that from personal contact with them I consider them to be a class of citizens of whom Canada might well be proud, a class of citizens who, given a fair opportunity, could be expected to succeed, if anybody could succeed, in this country. They met with some difficulty on the way here. They were delayed through storms on the ocean, through washouts on the railroad and other circumstances over which no one had control and as to which no fault can be attributed to anyone. They might have been pardoned, had they been inclined to take a somewhat gloomy view of this country, but the reverse was the case; when I met these men and women they were filled with hope, filled with optimism, filled with the ambition and the intention to succeed. They went on. They got to my own city of Red Deer, where they were intended to be located and where preparations had been made, to some extent at least, to receive them. A building of some considerable size in the vicinity of that city, which had been used as an Indian Industrial school, had been prepared for their accommodation in order that they might use it as their headquarters, from which they might go to secure the land they were desirous of obtaining and where their wives and families -because the greater number of the men were married men-might remain while the men were in search of land or of employment.
So far things had moved fairly smoothly. But a large number of these people who went there with such high hopes, hopes which were justified by the information they had received, are still in that building and unable to locate themselves upon the land which they had hoped to occupy. A great many of them are without funds, and from information I have received are dependent upon the charity of individuals. I believe that is a circumstance which is the most serious menace to our country that it is possible to conceive. We had a debate here-I am not going to quote from that debate, as I understand it would be against the rules of the House to do so-but we had a debate on immigration, in the course of which the need for immigration

Hebridean Immigrants
was stressed from all parts of the House. It was pointed out that Canada was a land of opportunity for desirable people who wished to come here. From this part of the House some notes of warning went forth; it was suggested that it was not sufficient to bring these people here, simply to land them in Canada and let them shift for themselves; that if they were brought here, adequate care should be taken to give them a proper opportunity to locate themselves and to build up their homes. Now, that was stressed, and I think, Mr. Speaker, that the situation which has evolved itself has proved the truth of that contention and proved it to the hilt.
There were, as I say, something over four hundred of this desirable class of immigrants many of whom were scattered between here [DOT]and their ultimate destination, taking up temporary employment in various provinces, but the majority of whom arrived at that city of Red Deer. Their destination was a part of the country which, I consider from my experience, to be a very good section indeed-a place where it is possible, if it is possible anywhere in the province, to succeed; a place largely devoted to mixed farming; a place where there is plenty of water, plenty of rain; a place where growth is usually assured year by year; a place where wood is available; a place pre-eminently suitable for small farmers and homesteaders, for men desirous of working in a concentrated way by putting in part of their time, possibly in assisting their neighbours who are farming on a larger scale-a place, I say, where if they could be properly established, they would have every chance of success.
In the statement which I placed before the House I made the assertion that some departmental responsibility was involved, and I consider, Mr. Speaker, that that assertion was well founded. What are the facts? In the first place this was a small selected body which we had hoped, and the department had hoped, would be the forerunner of a much larger body to come later. Long before these people came the department knew, at least roughly speaking, the number of people that might be expected; they knew that on account of the extensive advertising which had been given to this group of people, upon the reception accorded to them would depend to a large degree at least the success of any future immigration into Canada attempted from that part of the world. In these circumstances it seems to me it is the part of wisdom and common sense that the Department of Immigration should ensure, so far as humanly possible, the success of that detachment. More than that, these people came out here on information which they had received concerning this country. After this somewhat unfortunate situation had arisen, the gentleman in charge of the party was asked who he considered was to blame fo' what had happened, who was to- blame for these people not finding the conditions prevailing here that they had been led to believe they would find when they arrived here. They had been led to believe-and I am not saying they had been so informed directly by the Department of Immigration-that they would find a land where they could get free homesteads within reasonable distance of a railroad, or, as an alternative, where they could purchase land close to a railroad at low prices, on long term payments-terms which would not involve payment during the first one or two years. But when they came here they found the reverse was the case. As I say, the gentleman in charge of this party was asked who was to blame. He was not anxious to attach blame to anyone; he perhaps imputed some blame to himself, having been on the land in the first place to look over the situation. He said the information had been received in various ways, being partly contained in pamphlets furnished to these Hebrideans. He was asked:
Did the Western Canada Colonisation Association encourage these men in any way to come to Canada?
And he answered:
Yes; they sent out the pamphlets.
The further question was put:
Is that where these promises of land and homes and passage come from?
To which the answer was, "Yes." Now, it may be said that the government is not responsible for pamphlets issued by the Western Canada Colonization Association, and that might have been said with truth had it not been for the fact that by the granting of a sum of money to that company, the government to all intents and purposes became a co-partner with it in its endeavours. Having become a co-partner in that way, I contend that the department and the government-

speechtext: The hon. gentleman can rest content. I have had letters. I do not purpose reading them, because they were private letters; but they contained this information among other private information. I think the hon. member can take my word for it when I say I have had direct information from people at home with whom I am well acquainted, who have a knowledge of the facts from being on the ground,, and for whose character and the accuracy of whose information I can fairly -well vouch. But apart from that, I would like the hon. member to notice this: Whether right or wrong these things have gone out to the world through the press of this country, and no contradiction of any kind has been sent out by the Department of Immigration denying the truth of these statements, and it seems to me that if I had nothing to go on but the situation which has arisen from the accounts in the public press, it would still be a matter of public importance to bring it to the attention of this House. If the facts are not as stated here, then it seems to me the remedy is in the hands of the government and of the department, and that it was its duty to put a countervailing article in the pro's to contradict these things and give the facts as they are.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I am not discussing whether the immigrants went to the right place or not. I am not discussing whether the Department of Immigration should have encouraged them to go to Nova Scotia or not. I am discussing the situation which has arisen from the fact that these immigrants have gone into the vicinity of Red Deer in the province of Alberta. I am discussing the situation which has arisen and which at present exists, not any supposititious case.
Before I was interrupted by the hon. member I was speaking of the governmental responsibility involved. I was going on to say that whether the government had any responsibility for the pamphlets placed in these men's hands or not, whether or not these pamphlets were issued by the Western Canada Colonization Company has not very much to do with the main question, which is that the government, knowing these men were coming, should have seen to it that they knew the truth about the country before they set sail, and then having come here the problem before the government was-and they had ample time to prepare for it-to make sure before these people went to any district that they might find some place upon which they might set their feet, some land which they might take up.
We will go a little further. What is going to be the result of the situation which has arisen? Is it not going to be this, that the opinion will go abroad, and will rightly go abroad, that if this Department of Immigration is unable to successfully cope with the problem involved in bringing into Canada a limited number of selected immigrants of the best type, is unable to look after and locate four or five hundred people, then the department and this government cannot successfully cope with any extended immigration policy, cannot bring in, and locate, and in any way assist in settling, any large number of people?
35SS
Hebridean Immigrants

We are faced with a situation with two points of view. In the first place these people are suffering a hardship. They have been brought out to this country, rightly or wrongly, to a part of Canada where they ought to have a chance to achieve success, but they are now in a position where they see their hopes dwindling, where they see the small capital which they had saved in the Old Country disappearing, and when the time of the year they should get on the land is fast going by, and apparently

and I hope to be reassured on that point by the Minister of Agriculture-with no immediate prospects of relief in that direction. Apart from the hardship inflicted on these men what effect is their situation going to have on the men who, it was hoped, would follow them? It was hoped that a much larger number of their relatives and friends would follow them out here; but do you think, in view of the existing situation, in view of the difficulties these men are encountering, in view of the fact that they are unable to locate themselves, do you think for one moment that their relatives or friends, or neighbours will come out here and attempt to locate in Canada? I have noticed one or two editorials written on this subject. I hasten to say at once that I am not going to vouch for the accuracy of the editorials but I presume they reflect, in each case, the opinion of the editor and will be read and believed by at least a large part of the people of this country. The editorial I am about to quote is from the Calgary Albertan:
A couple of hundred Hebrideans, the very best type of new settlers have come from northern Scotland intending to make their homes in this province. They came with great expectations, hoping soon to be located upon their own farms, willing and anxious to make their own way by their own toil. They asked nothing but opportunity. Their hopes have not been realized. They have not been located. They are now living partly on charity in a somewhat congested and uncomfortable way in a large dormitory in or near to Red Deer. They are earning nothing and are eating up their small store.
Some one has blundered.
Who did make the mistake may be an interesting question which can be determined later on. The important problem just how is to get these people satisfactorily settled.
The editorial goes on to point out that the hope was entertained of getting further settlers by reason of the successful settlement of these men, and we come now to this point: Mistakes have been made whether by the Department of Immigration, whether by Father Macdonell, or whether by the men themselves to some extent I do not know at the present time. At any rate, mistakes have been made, this situation has arisen,

and I am hoping to hear, later on, what the Department of Immigration intends to do to alleviate the existing condition and to bring in possibly more men of this desirable type. These editorials are being circulated throughout the country. I read another one in a Saskatchewan paper; I am not going to read it but it is practically along the same line. "More blundering" is what they say in the headline and they emphasize what was stated in this House.

The editorial to which I am now alluding appeared in the Saskatoon Daily Star of June 2nd. It says:
The 300-
The editorial says 300 but the figures are not correct; however the essential part of the editorial is correct.
-sold their holdings in the old land, according to their statement, in the expectation that they would find cultivated homesteads, on easy terms of payment and close to a railroad, awaiting them. Instead of forming a colony, as they had anticipated, they will he scattered. The long term loans promised them will not be forthcoming. They find that cultivated farm land near transportation facilities has a higher value than they believed and that it must be at least partly paid for on occupation.
Something which we who live in this country, which anybody familiar with the country, could have told them before they left the Old Land. Then they could have come prepared to meet those conditions. The editorial is correct.
The Hebrideans will make a success of their venture. No one will say that they do not share the opportunities -which are the privilege of every western citizen.
I hope that prophecy is true.
But why were they deceived? Are delusion and
overstatement the only means of bringing people to this country? If the truth about western Canada is so unsavory that it cannot be told to a prospective emigrant from the Old World, then the sooner it reverts to the Indians the better.
That is what this editorial says and that is what we contend. We do not say that the . country is only fit for Indians, but that if you cannot get settlers here by telling the truth as to the conditions they will find when they get here so that they shall be prepared when they do come to adapt themselves to those conditions, it is far better not to have them come here at all. It would have been far better for them to have stayed in the land from which they came than to have moved to Canada and find themselves in such a mess as they have got into now. Because it is the effect of the experience of these men that

Hebridean Immigrants
we have got to reckon with in connection with our immigration policy. Now, I have no doubt other hon. members who are interested in this subject will be anxious to take part in this debate. Because of that and because I wish to give the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization a fair opportunity of stating the other side of the case from a departmental point of view, and bearing in mind the fact that I shall have an opportunity of closing the debate and concluding my remarks, if I think it necessary, I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your courtesy and take my seat.

speechtext:
I may say at the outset that I am going to be brief and probably that statement will afford ground for applause. But as a representative of the province of Nova Scotia which, in all matters which are dealt with at Ottawa, may be considered the province that was passed by, I rise to say this: When the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) referred to Father Macdonell endeavouring to bring emigrants to this country the only mistake made was that they did not locate in the province of Nova Scotia. These people come from the Hebrides, a portion of Scotland where they are used to engaging in divers occupations. If they had come to the province of Nova Scotia they would have an opportunity to fish and also to farm on a small scale. We are not asking for special concessions for the province of Nova Scotia. All that we do ask is this- that in so far as immigrants are concerned the people of that province shall be treated in exactly the same way as other portions of the Dominion. The unfortunate thing in connection with our immigration policy, it seems to me is that when we ask for immigrants they are required to go out to the prairies. Men who are used to fishing, men who are sailors, men who had small places of their own on the ocean shore, are required to go out to western Canada and become progressive farmers; whereas such men.as these coming from Scotland should be located in the province of Nova Scotia where they can 229
engage in fishing for certain portions of the year, where they can engage in farming or other occupations, where they are likely to make a success. The most desirable place for people from Scotland is in the old province of Nova Scotia. They hail from old ScQtland and it would be well if they settled in new Scotland. I say that although I do not claim to be a Scotchman.

Any man who is actuated by desire to make a good living for himself and his family, and with a desire to have his family educated, cannot find a better place in the whole live world than the little province of Nova Scotia. My hon. friend from Prince Edward Island might prefer the conditions in his province, but the conditions there are very much the same as ours. We have the finest fruit growing country in the world and the finest fishing-

speechtext:
The motion for adjournment for a special purpose gives rise to discussion under well-defined rules. I would call attention of hon. members of the House to paragraph C, subsection 7, rule 39, which says-
The motion must not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the same session.

Hebridean Immigrants

The discussion on the motion can only be on the lines of the matter of urgent public importance. There are several rulings on this matter. At page 105 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary rules and forms, I find the following:
A motion under this rule must be restricted to a single specific matter of recent occurence; and as the matter to be discussed must be of an urgent nature, no notice should be given of an intention to resort to the motion on a future occasion.
The point is that there is restriction in the debate to the matter which is under consideration. The whole question of immigration cannot be brought up in the discussion. The question introduced on this occasion has been clearly explained by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) as a matter of urgent public importance. That is the only question before the House. No advertisement of any special province for immigration purposes could be the subject of this debate. I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the question before the House.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I bow to the ruling, but I think the hon. member for Red Deer in the course of his disquisition was intending to criticize the government for things that occurred in regard to immigration. If I misunderstood it, then I apologize to you Mr Speaker, and bow to your' ruling, for which I have the deepest respect. But when the hon. member undertakes to criticize Father Macdonell for what he has done, I wish to say that the province of Nova Scotia would approve of what he has done and would welcome all these immigrants.

speechtext:
The hon. member is apt to criticize everything the Minister of the Interior does. All I have to say to him is this-and I do not want to get away from the question before the House-that the people of Canada are absolutely 4 p.m. satisfied with what the minister is doing. He is doing his best and no man can do more, as the saying goes. My hon. friend could not be satisfied with anything the Minister of the Interior did at all. Now Mr. Speaker, I am not going to discuss this matter. But seeing that my hon. friends opposite are somewhat selfish in their interests, all I have to say is that, irrespective of what the motion may be, if the rest of this country 	; '
are not prepared to take Father Macdonell's immigrants, the county of Hants-I need not say anything about Nova Scotia-will take them all, because they are sturdy highlanders and are quite willing and able to make their living in any sphere of life in which God may place them. I have nothing more to say beyond this, that I want the whole question considered on its merits. And when the hon. member undertakes to move the adjournment of the House to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, I think he should have something of greater interest than the discussion of something that pertains simply to the particular constituency of Red Deer, where he wants people to settle, but he does not want the proper people to go there.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Before the minister replies, I wish to put a question which he might answer. I have been fully informed by the friends of Father Mao-donell as to his whole plan, and I am very much surprised to hear the information that has been given to us by the hon. member for Red Deer. The minister will remember that an important delegation waited upon him, including the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin), the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) and sotme others, and laid down a plan for taking care of the men whom Father Macdonell was bringing over. I think the information given to the minister was that an organization had been completed clear across the continent, so that those men who are coming out under his auspices would be taken care of perhaps better than any other group of immigrants that have ever come to Canada, I would like the minister, when he replies to the question put by the hon. member for Red Deer, to tell us whether this organization that Father Macdonell created has fallen .to pieces, or whether he still hopes to make it operative, so that the men he brings out will be taken care of as he promised, as we all hope they will be; and if he will fulfil his part of the undertaking that he entered into with the Minister of the Interior.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil, Acting Minister of Immigration):
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of any definite scheme of the character the hon. member has described. True, Father Macdonell has made representations to organizations that were sympathetic for the purpose of securing money to loan, to establish his immigrants upon land, and they had made considerable progress. I cannot say that it is fulfilled, because outside of having a knowledge of it, I was not consulted about the matter particularly further than that I knew it was a general scheme of loaning money to establish newcomers on land by an organization interested in their welfare; but as to the scheme suggested by my hon. friend, I must confess I did not hear it, because when I became acquainted with Father Macdonell he was bringing people to Ontario and establishing them on farms, and they were being brought from the very locality in which those settlers who are now located at Red Deer were recruited. He seemed to be achieving considerable success, and was anxious to branch out in a larger way. I say frankly that, so far as my knowledge goes. Father Macdonell is one of the most successful colonizers we have working to-day in behalf of immigration and colonization. I shall deal briefly with the question raised by my hon. friend in reference to this party of Hebrideans who have come 229 i
to Canada under the auspices of the Rev. Father Macdonell and the Rev. Father MacIntyre. My hon. friend has laid considerable stress on the advertising generally which induced these people to come to Canada, and he declares that he cannot but hold the Department of Immigration responsible for that publicity. Very well; so far so good. I may say to my hon. friend and to the House too, that this is a matter of which I have been somewhat apprehensive myself. I do not think that we can possibly exercise too great care in controlling the advertising matter sent out, and I would not say for a moment that copies of the scheme of settlement of the Canada Colonization Association did not reach these settlers. I will say, however, and say it most emphatically, that never at any time did the Canada Colonization Association have anything to do with the movement of that party, apart from discussing with Father Macdonell the possibility of their assistance. And if the scheme of the Canada Colonization Association got to Scotland, if copies of it reached the hands of these settlers, it may have been carried to them by the party who came here last summer, who are now associated with these settlers, and who, I take it, would give first-hand information with regard to what they have seen in Canada. In order that the people might have an accurate knowledge of the conditions in Canada, I have been pleased on every occasion to place at the disposal of the representatives of settlers, in any locality on the continent or in Great Britain, who desired to look the situation over, every facility to study conditions in this country. Last year the Holland government sent a representative directly representing it in the person of Baron Sandberg, who travelled through Canada, being in charge of immigration work for the authorities in Holland. He gained information at first hand and from actual observation while in Canada. The government of Italy sent out Miss Garibaldi who travelled throughout Canada and carried back to her country personal knowledge of conditions here. The government of Switzerland was represented by Mr. Fitz Beck, who went from one part of this country to the other investigating, on his own behalf, conditions as they actually exist in Canada. And I know of no better way for the people who intend to come to this country to get information than from their own representatives who are engaged in the work of immigration and colonization and who come here to investigate matters for themselves.
The Immigration department cannot be responsible for all sorts of representations that
Hebridean Immigrants

are made regarding conditions in Canada- that is an utter impossibility. There are thousands of people interested in selling land in Canada; there are private individuals who are anxious to further sales. Why, I was so eager to ascertain from my hon friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) whether Father Mac-donell had really made the statements attributed to him in the press, why I wished to nail the allegations down, was simply because I myself have been constantly in touch with Father Macdonell with respect to the difficulties he has experienced at Red Deer. Last year, in common with the other persons I have referred to, four farmers from Barra and South Uist, from which these settlers come, visited Canada under the auspices of Father Macdonell and travelled through the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, carrying out a thorough investigation, And they are four members of the present party who are here to-day.
Now, I am willing to assume all the responsibility that my hon. friends would place upon me, and I have taken the greatest precautions to see that those people who are coming to Canada as immigrants shall be given exact information as to the conditions they may expect. But there is one unfortunate circumstance that we must take note of, and that is the fact that too many decided to come at once. Let me state, however, that more than half of these people are comfortably settled; more than half of them have been established since coming to Canada, and twelve families of them will be settled in the next day or two at Westlock and twelve more at Ohaton.
I say most emphatically, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a particle of criticism coming to the department or any of its officials in connection with this matter, and I defy hon. gentlemen, either on this side of the House or on the other, or anywhere else for that matter, to adduce any definite evidence to show that on a single occasion we have failed to carry out to the fullest extent any promise we made with respect to the settlement of these people. At their disposal have been placed two of the soldier settlement inspectors, and Mr. Boyd, the superintendent in charge of western Canada, has been on the ground ever since they arrived, offering whatever assistance is within his power. Furthermore, because these people are largely of the Roman Catholic faith, I apealed directly to the Bishop of Edmonton, who is interested in their settlement, and who accordingly has sent a representative to work in conjunction with us in the endeavour properly to establish them. I firmly declare that a large part of the discontent that has arisen among 
some of these people who are not already settled has been engendered through influence from outside sources, by persons who are not responsible. Such persons go to these settlers and suggest that they should be on free homestead land. God knows, Mr. Speaker, I should be delighted to put them on homesteads if I could; and we did secure positions at Winnipeg and elsewhere, for all those who desired to take them. But these people are anxious to settle in a colony, which is natural, of course; and this is one of the difficulties we have to cope with. I want to assure the House quite positively that I have no complaint to make concerning them. 'They are a splendid type of people and I trust we shall be able to assist them to adapt themselves completely to their new surroundings. Naturally, however, this is somewhat difficult of achievement just yet; they are in a strange country and in a new environment. If any one of us were transplanted into such changed conditions and new atmosphere we should certainly be homesick for a while.
I might state at this stage that the abandoned buildings and land at Red Deer, of the old Indian school, which was utilized for some years for the training of soldiers who Were to be placed on the land, we have now equipped and placed at the disposal of the settlers that they might be comfortable. The four farmers who came here last year, after looking the country over, decided that, from the standpoint of the settlers, the broken country was preferable to the park-like localities. The broken country was perhaps more akin to the land from which they were coming. But these four representatives were delighted with the land; I know, because they were in my office and had a personal conversation with me before going back to Scotland. I do not know that anything else could have been done by us. I do not think we have left undone anything that we might have done. It is true that not all the women and children have been moved from the Red Deer headquarters to their homes on which the men have been established. That has taken some time, and will take some time yet. Probably it will be July 1 before the last members of the party are settled. But the fact that they have found the land perhaps higher in price than they had been led to believe; the probability that stories had been told them that inspired the expectation that there were homes that they could walk into; and the further fact that they have no live stock and little or no capital, have all had a tendency to create a feeling of unrest among them.
Then, when they are told: "You should not be established in this way, you should go on

Hebridean Immigrants
a homestead," they become absolutely dissatisfied. ' Let me ask my hon. friends who have gone through the homesteading experience in western Canada: Is it a good thing to take a stranger who has no money and place him with his wife and perhaps seven or eight children thirty or forty miles away on a prairie homestead? What earthly chance would he and his family have? I do not believe that that is the proper way to encourage people to come into this country. But there are others who hold the contrary view and say to these newcomers, "You should not take this load of indebtedness upon your shoulders, rather you should secure a grant of land."
We have been endeavouring to give these immigrants the best possible advice, we have placed at their disposal our officials, trained in the business of settling people on the land, and we are leaving no stone unturned to make them comfortable and happy. To be frank, when I heard that 416 souls were coming out together I had doubts about the advisability of so many coming in one party. I do not think they should come in parties of more than 25, which is about the size we can handle most satisfactorily. I do not wish it to be inferred that every new settler will be given the same personal assistance that we are giving to this particular body of immigrants, for I do not think the government could afford to do so, but inasmuch as I believe in what my hon. friend has said, that the best propagandist you can have is a satisfied settler, I have deemed it advisable to see that everything humanly possible should be done by our officials to settle these people comfortably and satisfactorily. Not only that, but I sent Mr. Black, the deputy minister of the department, to Red Deer in order that he might bring to me firsthand information of what is going on, although we are in daily communication with our officials who are already there. I have his wire, sent yesterday, in -which he states:
Settlement Hebridean party proceeding satisfactorily. Utmost assistance consistent with their ultimate welfare being given.
I expect to .receive a detailed report from Mr. Black within the next day or two, but from what I have heard from Father Mac-donell he expects to have every one of these people comfortably settled upon the land.
I do not say for a single moment that there are not some members of this party who have become dissatisfied. They are extremely desirous of settling in a solid community. I need only repeat what I have said on many other occasions, that I am not particularly favourable to such a settlement. I think a
man has a better chance of success if he will go in amongst people who know the country and how to take advantage of the local conditions. In this way newcomers quickly learn to adapt themselves to their new environment and are much better off among those already settled on the land than in a solid community of their own people where they are likely to be constantly meeting and discussing real or imaginary grievances, which has a tendency to make them dissatisfied with their new home. Our officials are endeavouring to settle these people in the way I have suggested and to settle them comfortably. True, these newcomers have not very much money, and I am well aware that they will have a somewhat trying time at the start, as all new settlers do; probably they will go through the same experience that many of us went through-many a night I slept under the wagon when I could not get to my house, and I did not have a very comfortable house at that-and I am not speaking of something I do not know anything about. But, unfortunately, if people are encouraged to think they are coming to a bed of roses, that everything is going to be made easy for them and that they will have no difficulties to overcome, there is bound to be trouble and disappointment.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say most emphatically that nothing has been left undone in our efforts to help these people. We have kept constantly in touch with the situation. Some newspapers are prone to spread propaganda rather than take the trouble to investigate the facts. To say that we are not having difficulties would be a stretch of the imagination. Of course we are having difficulties, and I expect to have more, in fact we are bound to have difficulties as long as we are engaged in this work; but I have no apologies to make on behalf of the men in the Department of Immigration for the way in which they have handled the four hundred Hebridean immigrants to this country.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a Scottish immigrant I may be allowed to engage in this discussion. Although I know very well that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) is anxious for the welfare and prosperity of these immigrants, I was glad to see the minister (Mr. Stewart) reply with such vigour, because it may be that he has not been getting just exactly fair play. I quite agree with what he says as to the difficulties newcomers will have to surmount, the trials they will have to undergo and perhaps the heartaches they will have to suffer, before they succeed. But I am not saying this to
Hebridean Immigrants

let the Department of Immigration down easily, because I do believe they need to be very critical of the class of people they bring into this country and to be very careful to look after them thoroughly once they reach here. My only reason for speaking is that I have on my desk a few lines which seem to me appropriate in connection with what the Minister of Immigration said about the heartaches and homesickness of these new immigrants, and I now quote them:
From the lone sheiling of the misty Island; Mountains divide us, and the waste of seas;
Yet still the blood is strong, the heart is Highland, And we in dreams behold the Hebrides.
Fair these broad meads-the hoary woods are grand, But we are exiles from our fathers' land.
That portrays faithfully the feelings of these people. I am not a Highlander myself, but I know a little about the Highland temperament. The Highlander has a poetic temperament, and I know very well that when he comes to Canada he is very apt to get just a little downhearted amid his strange surroundings. On the other hand there is a resilience in the Highland nature that will quickly come on the rebound, and I am confident that you will find these men and women making good in the not very far distant future. From the way in which the minister has spoken to-day I am sure he will see to it that his department does everything possible to assist these immigrants, and I can only hope that they will become so well satisfied in their new homes that there will be a continual stream of these Highlanders coming to Canada-the Scotland of North America.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am quite satisfied that the department has done a great deal for these immigrants, but I think it should have gone somewhat further with advice. There is one side of this matter that perhaps some hon. members may not know. These immigrants come from the island of Lewis, and some of us are aware that this island was purchased, some years ago by Lord Leverhulme, who ever since has been endeavouring to get these people to fish or to emigrate. He believes that they should go to work and fish in the interests of Lord Leverhulme, who at the present time is trying to establish fish markets for his particular benefit, having already acquired control of the manufacture of soap in the Old Country. Therefore he is telling these people to move off to the coast and fish in his interests or get out of the island. That is another side of the matter which should interest parliament, and I would therefore ask the minister to put forth every possible effort to see that these 
people are suitably settled in this country. They are the people who have supplied their full quota of sailors to the British navy, they are loyalists to the extreme and make the very best class of citizens. I cannot understand their spirit if they are giving up now or becoming disheartened; that is not a quality that can be attributed to the Scottish people of the past. I believe that if these people are given support and encouragement they will make good. But like the member for Hants (Mr. Martell) I think that a mistake has been made. You cannot take the men of that part of the Highlands which are close to the sea, close to the smell of the water, and put them out on a plain and expect them to make good. They will in time drift to the water or to their compatriots; and if there is any trouble now it will be to the interest of this country for the department to assist these people and place them where they will be situated close to their compatriots. I appeal on behalf of Father Macdonell, who was with us in the service at the front, who is an enthusiastic Scot and a Briton, and who is seeking only to see that these people are comfortably established. I have no doubt that he knows well the history of the people on that island and he will endeavour to see that those who come here are placed in this country where they will make good. These facts are worth bringing to the attention of the minister, and I hope he will see that if these people are not satisfied at Red Deer they will be taken to some other part of the country and placed where they will make good rather than be permitted to go to the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) thought it necessary to move the adjournment of the House to discuss a subject based upon an alleged interview in a newspaper as responsible-or as irresponsible, if you choose to put it that way-as the Calgary Albertan. We all want immigration; is this the way to get it? It looks to me as if my good friend the member for Red Deer was looking for trouble rather than an alleviation of trouble. His whole attitude, the tone that he adopted, bespoke a belligerency that perhaps he did not intend. His intimation that these settlers are discouraged is not a surprise to me. If my hon. friend makes speeches out in Red Deer the way he does in this House and the way some other hon. members from Alberta do, then I am not surprised that these settlers get discouraged. I was an im-

Hebridean Immigrants
migrant to that western country; I went from Portage la Prairie when there was not a foot of railway between that place and the Pacific.
I know how easy it is to discourage immigrants. I know that people who went out there often started back, homesick; possibly it was the first time they had ever left their home fireside. When these Hebrideans, with a strong attachment for their fireside and their country, finding themselves for the first time in a strange land, are told yams such as are floating round in the newspapers of Alberta, is it any wonder that they are discouraged? As a matter of fact, I have been expecting exactly this thing to happen ever since I heard that these splendid Scottish settlers had gone to Red Deer. What is the nature of the environment there; what is the atmosphere with respect to immigration? What is the attitude of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and of the hon. member for Battle river (Mr. Spencer) with respect to immigration? Have they encouraged immigrants to go there? Have they held out to them the right hand of fellowship when they got there? What has been their general attitude? If these immigrants have read some of the speeches made by the hon. member for Bow River or the hon. member for Red Deer, it is no wonder they have the blues and feel like going back to Scotland. Until hon. gentlemen from Alberta take a different attitude toward immigration and toward these various questions that arise, they are going to be a long while settling the plains of the West from any source whatever.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? He has suggested that the result of some speeches made by members from Alberta has been to discourage immigrants. Is it not likely that the rosy speeches made by Mr. Duncan Marshall in the Old Country, when he was describing conditions in Alberta, and then the actual conditions that the people found when they got there, have been more likely to cause discouragement than any attempt on the part of hon. members from Alberta to portray the facts?

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I did not see any statement by Mr. Duncan Marshall to the effect that my hon. friend describes. If he will let me know what the statements were -I know he was run over by a steer or something of that kind; is that what my hon. friend refers to?

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I was referring to the fact that in the literature of the
Western Canada Colonization Association it was stated that Mr. Duncan Marshall was over in the Old Land drumming for settlers.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend is driving at; it seems to me he is pretty hard put to it for something to chew about. The hon. member for Red Deer asked the question, can the government be relied upon to engage in any considerable scheme of immigration? And he based that question upon an alleged interview published in a newspaper. There is no question that the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer, whether they were so intended or not, could not be accepted in any other way than as a straight attack upon the Department of the Interior. I think the whole incident has been most disgraceful, Mr. Speaker. We will never get anywhere in the development of our country and the settling of unoccupied lands if this kind of attitude is taken by hon. members. The whole situation as 1 see it is not one for us to get into an argument over here in this House. I have no desire in any way to criticize the minister unfairly or to get him in wrong, if I may use the expression, in the portion of the country from which he comes, but if an unsatisfactory condition does exist I think he should be anxious to lend his assistance and that of the department in an endeavour to remedy it.
I was about to say when I was last interrupted, that if we are going to have agents in Europe to encourage people to come here, in my hum-

Hebridean Immigrants
ble opinion it is necessary to have agents in the West to look after them when they arrive. There was a time several years ago when our two hon. ministers who have spoken homesteaded in the West. Homesteading then could be done very cheaply. But that day is past. The cost of equipment and of living while they are waiting to be settled has greatly increased, the cost of the land has increased, and unless these people have a considerable sum of money with them there is no prospect so far as I can see for them to immediately settle on the land and make good; and unless the department is prepared to have some organization that will take care of these people for the first few7 months I cannot see any prospect of evading this trouble. I would appeal to the minister, unless he is entirely convinced that conditions are not as represented in that press report, that he lend his influence and the influence of his department to making the conditions at least somewhat better than they are.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Acting Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I shall not detain the House more than a few moments. I happen to be a son of the Macdonalds of the Hebrides islands. My forefathers came to this country 160 years ago. They came to what was then an unknown land. They landed in Nova Scotia and they had no buildings prepared for them; the land was not ready for the plough; they had to go into the forest and cut down the trees to build their houses. Then they had to clear the land. Day by day and year by year hundreds of these men and women endured these hardships. Then there came in a continuous stream of other men from the Hebrides and the Western islands and peopled the whole of eastern Nova Scotia. The men who came in after years had to go through all these privations that the first settlers endured. There was nobody there representing the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment or any other governmental institution to look after them when they arrived. They fought their way along and they gave to Canada, to the church and along educational lines the leading men of the Dominion for the last seventy-five years. There are more men and women speaking Gaelic in eastern Nova Scotia than there are in the whole Western islands to-day. This year, within a month, we are celebrating the 150th anniversary of the landing of these first Scotch settlers in the town where I have the honour to live and the county I have the honour to represent. I mention this fact because as one who has read the history of the privations of these men and women and the story of their wonderful achievement, I sometimes wonder whether the men of this twentieth century are built of the same fibre as the stalwart men and women of one hundred and fifty years ago, and I would ask the House in considering the situation of these sons of the Hebrides who have come here in these later days to make a comparison in some slight degree between the difficulties they may be undergoing for the moment and the hardships which their fellow-clansmen endured and the difficulties they overcame over one hundred and fifty years ago.
I had the pleasure of meeting Father Mac-donell on his way to the West, I hpd not had the opportunity of meeting him before. I discussed with him, being a Highlander myself, the story of the Macdonald highlanders and the genus of the race from which he and the men whom he was taking to the West sprang. I pointed out to him that, as the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) has said, the Highlander is naturally a mystic. He is born under the conditions outlined in the poem which the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) so aptly quoted, and it is under such conditions that the genus of the race has developed. When these people are transplanted to the foothills of the Rockies, knowing the sentiments they entertain towards the land of their forefathers, transplanted into a community which is utterly foreign and where conditions are vastly different from those they have been accustomed to from boyhood-*

the great necessity of taking better care of immigrants when they come to this country than has been the policy of governments of the past. Now, no better class of emigrants can come to this country than people from Scotland, and in this connection I wish to draw attention to a statement I noticed in the press this morning from Mr. Woods, an editor of Alberta. I know nothing about this gentleman's politics, or anything of that sort, but he condemns Canada very severely. He has just returned from a trip to the Old Land and he condemns Canada very severely for not taking her proper place in looking after just such settlers as these, settlers from Scotland; in not attempting to get enough of them in comparison with the attempts being made by Australia and New Zealand. And he goes on to make the statement that to-day in the British Isles, Australia has taken the foremost position which Canada occupied up till very recently in the estimation of the people of Britain, because of the lack of energy that we have shown in going after and getting British emigrants for this country, which lack of energy he claims has been particularly shown at the present time. However, it is not that I wish to point out, I wish to impress upon the government that the utmost should be done when we get immigrants to come to this country to look after them on their arrival. The old methods of the past- and all governments pursued those methods -cannot be followed at the present time in this country. Canada must in the future when she gets immigrants-

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE

I just wished to emphasize that, because although I have listened to other speakers I did not notice any of them emphasizing the point as strongly as I am attempting to do. If the statements are incorrect they should be denied. Some of these settlers have been placed in our neighbourhood in the province of Ontario, within the last couple of months, under the direction of the Ontario Department of Agriculture. In conversation with the farmers who are employing these men they give the very highest recommendation of the qualifications for service. One farmer in particular, only a couple of weeks ago, stated
to me that the man he had employed was one of the finest hands he had ever had in his service. The only difficulty the farmers encountered was that of understanding the language of their help because they use the Gaelic. These men are doing good service and they are happy and contented.

I am just coming to

I think the criticism that has been offered is well worthy of the attention of the minister. I hope either that something will be done to correct these statements if they are wrong, or else that the conditions complained of will be corrected.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
As a scion of one of these Scotch emigrants families that came to the Maritime provinces over a century ago, I may be pardoned for making an observation or two on this matter before the debate closes. Apparently most of the speakers are stressing the point that these emigrants are dissatisfied. They are trying to make of this a social question and not an economic one. As I understand the situation from the speech of the hon. member for Red Deer this is purely an economic question. These men are stranded in Red Deer, and they are without work, they have no opportunity of going on the land; it is not a matter of not being satisfied with the social conditions or anything of that sort. It seems to me that hon. members are approaching it entirely from the wrong angle. I think if there is anything to learn from a condition of this kind, it is that people without money should never be brought into the country, unless adequate provision has been made for settling them on the land. The Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) drew an analogy between this and the condition of his ancestors and mine also, when they settled in the Maritime provinces over a century ago. There are differences and very great differences. Those people who went in there in the early days were brought there by an organization. Arrangements were made for settling them on the land. They did not have to buy the land. They were
Hebridean Immigrants

either given it free or allowed to rent land partly prepared for them, where settlement had already been made. Those conditions do not prevail in Alberta at the present time. There is no free land there. They must buy it. Unless some provision is made under the Soldier Settlement Board plan, or some plan of that kind, people should never be brought in, unless there is work for them. I think the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), speaking in the House some time ago, advised the government to adopt some such plan as that. Until such a plan is adopted, and until the government is prepared to come forward with some such policy, it is nothing short of folly to bring people in under these circumstances. I rather resent the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) toward the hon. member for Red Deer. There is a certain kind of bird which, when it is pursued and threatened with danger, sticks its head in the sand and thinks all trouble is over. That is the attitude of the minister. He is evading the issue and trying to ignore, rather than to face it.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
As I understand the matter under discussion as introduced by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), it is that, according to report, some hundreds of Hebrideans, who were brought to this country seemingly under the joint efforts of Father Macdonell, the colonization scheme of this country and the Dominion government, are suffering and in great straits. I notice the matter has been received in this House as might have been expected, when we reflect upon the fact that the condition of these immigrants is a striking criticism of the present government's immigration policy, 'and also a vindication of the statement that has been 5 p.m. made from this side of the House when the policy of the government was under discussion. And now the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) denies this report. He challenges the statement of the hon. member for Red Deer and passes it by as merely a newspaper report of some ill-advised or evil-minded individual. May I challenge that statement of the minister? May I say that some days ago I took sufficient interest in this question to wire to several sources in Alberta to acertain the truth of the matter. I wired to an official of the Alberta government and asked two questions. I asked, first, if the Alberta government had been approached to give relief to these people, and,' second, if the press report could be relied upon. The reply came

back that, while the government had not been appealed to by Father Macdonell or the officials of the group, yet it had been appealed to by individuals of that group, and the reply also said that the press reports were undeniably true.

To say that only five men of that group of hundreds are dissatisfied is, in my opinion, to state something that is wide of the mark, and I think the minister has been misinformed in that regard. It has been that attitude which has characterized the government on several questions throughout this session and throughout last session. The hon. Minister of the Interior, as I have said, disregards this, and thinks it is merely a story. Then the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) comes along and tells us that he is related to these poor men and women in some far-off way, and that his own ancestors came from the same country some hundreds of years ago. That ought to comfort the Hebridean immigrants. He also tells them that they belong to a great race that has contributed the leading lights, politically and otherwise of this country. I have no doubt at all that will comfort them greatly. But the hon. minister brings forward no proposal that will help to meet the present situation. He brings forward no suggestion that will relieve the pressure from which these men are suffering. He simply smiles at them and says "Remember that you have come from a great country." And that reminds me also of the country they did come from. It reminds me of the sad and tragic conditions which partly led them to leave their country. I am not blaming this government entirely for the fact that all these people came over here. They came from a country that had been oppressed. They came from a little island that was bought out by Lord Leverhulme, the soap man. He bought out their island-

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and will leave that point. I had intended showing its bearing upon their position at the present time, but inasmuch as I cannot do so without contravening your ruling I must necessarily abandon the point. I will continue my remarks in respect to the attitude of the government towards this situation. I have referred to the treatment meted out by the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald); now I will consider for a moment the consolation that has been offered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). In the first place he criticizes severely the hon. member for Red Deer for having brought the matter before the House; and not content with that meed of consolation, he makes an attack upon a reputable newspaper for having dared to publish the truth in this matter. The hon. gentleman referred to the Morning Albertan; but I observed that the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart), who knows that newspaper and its editor a good deal better than does the Minister of Agriculture, did not take the same course. That is the contribution of the Minister of Agriculture to the discussion. Then the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) informs us that he saw in a paper some time ago that some immigrants in some other country had met with some difficulty. Well, that ought to meet the situation; if it does not, I do not see where we can look for better advice.
Now, Mr. Speaker, assertions of this sort will not help matters at all. I want to congratulate the membere for Red Deer on having introduced the subject, and I only regret that he did not bring it up when we were going into Supply in order that it might have been taken a little more seriously. This is a matter which touches very closely the policy of the present administration; it reveals a weakness somewhere in their policy, if they have one. It is indeed a tragic beginning of the activities of the Immigration department, which has been subsidized by such a large sum of money from the public treasury. If the object of voting money for immigration was to bring immigrants into the country, then the direct result that has so far been attained has been simply to nullify all the immigration propaganda that could possibly be put out for some years to come. I want to ask the Acting Minister of Immigration to give some assurance to the House at this time that the condition of these people will be investigated immediately by his department, and that relief will be sent them according to their requirements.
