speechtext: I thought I gave that assurance. Did I not tell the members of this House that the Soldier Settlement Board had been working among them ever since they arrived? Did I not tell him as well that representatives of the church were there? Did I not state that Mr. Black, the deputy minister, had been there? If the hon. gentleman has anything further to suggest that might be done I shall be glad to hear what it is.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I have got some other things to suggest. But it seems to me that if all these things that the minister states have already been done, then there must be inefficiency somewhere, because the results are not yet apparent. If the gentlemen referred to by the minister had been sent out to investigate matters, it ought to have been evident before now what action had been taken, before the newspaper reports to which reference has been made were published. Let me read a short extract from the Morning Bulletin of Edmonton dealing with the subject. This is a paper which neither the Minister of Agriculture nor the Acting Minister of Immigration will question. Under the caption "Investigation Needed", it states:
Alberta's new residents from the Hebrides Islands are said to be not altogether satisfied wih the treatment they have received, and are inclined to think that there is a difference between the conditions as represented to them and the conditions as they exist. It is not uncommon for a new comer to any strange country to find that the reality does not in all respects coincide with the impression he had formed and brought with him. All the same, these complaints should be looked into promptly and carefully by officials of the immi-

Hebridean Immigrants
gration department, and full and ample justice done to these settlers. If things have been misrepresented to them they will have to be compensated in some way by somebody. Canada is a good enough country for anyone, without having its conditions and opportunities exaggerated in the hope of drawing immigrants; and to permit that is about the surest way to neutralize immigration effort and waste the public money spent on it. The Dominion government would not of course be a party to such misrepresentation, and it cannot afford to allow other parties to bring people here by such means.
There is a suggestion in the latter part of the editorial that the government seems^ to have delegated its power to other organizations and now seeks to disclaim all responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Does the
hon. gentleman really imply that the government are trying to evade their responsibility? That is the practical statement that he makes. Does he mean to imply anything of the kind? Or is he making a positive statement?

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I said that the policy of the government was such that it could enable them to escape responsibility and blame somebody else. I think I heard the minister this afternoon say that he was willing to accept all responsibility in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I am.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: What more do you want?

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I want a little more than the accepting of responsibility on the part of the minister; I want the carrying out of that responsibility with regard to these people who are suffering. And if the minister who has just asked me a question has anything better to offer than we have had from the Acting Minister of Immigration I am sure the House would be glad to hear him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I emphatically deny that the people are suffering at all; I deny that a single one is suffering. 1 challenge the hon. gentleman to name one who has suffered up to this moment.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: That is a very safe challenge for the minister to throw down; he can very safely dare me to name one of four hundred persons not one of whom I have ever seen and of not one of whom I have any personal knowledge.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: It is an unsafe challenge when the man knows what he is talking about.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I will not accept as a challenge that which is an impossibility. But I want to state that I am just as firm in my belief that a great number of these people

are suffering as the minister is convinced that they are not. I challenge him to give us the proof of his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I cannot allow that statement to go unchallenged. Irresponsible statements of this character have been made in the House and I have sat in my place and disregarded them, not considering it worth my while to refute them. That day is past, however. No longer will I allow, if I can possibly prevent it, statements of the kind to be made by any hon. gentleman without contradiction. I say now that not a single member of the party in question has suffered in consequence of any laxity on the part of the government; further, I make the positive statement that none of them are suffering now. They are all comfortably housed and will be so housed until such time as they are permanently settled.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: The minister declares that no one of these people has suffered because of any action or inaction on the part of the government. Does he say that they have not suffered at all, for any reason whatever? Am I to understand that not a single one has suffered; that the whole charge is utterly baseless; that the advice of Hon. Alex Ross of the Alberta government is not founded on anything substantial; and that the newspaper reports are all false? What evidence has the minister to give us in support of his sweeping denial ?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: There is a vast difference between suffering and dissatisfaction. Surely the hon. gentleman will admit that. The hon. gentleman is attempting to convey the impression that the people are suffering. The suggestion is entirely erroneous, and not in its wildest flights of imagination has any newspaper made it.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: If the minister will read some of the newspaper reports he will find it stated that Father Macdonell, out of his own pocket, is feeding a hundred and tw'enty-five of them. If that does not suggest the idea of suffering, then I do not know what the minister would regard as the meaning of that word. I am not going to engage in a debate with the hon. minister as to what he means by "suffering.' I submit that disappointment is the keenest kind of suffering.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Father Macdonell is a paid official of this government, and if he is disbursing money out of his own pocket this government will repay it. Father Macdonell is in charge of this party, and we are holding him responsible. He is acting

Hebridean Immigrants
on behalf of the government of Canada. I do hope my hon. friend will be more careful about the statements he makes because I do not propose to let unfounded assertions go unchallenged.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am just as careful about the statements I make as is the hon. minister himself, and I am just as particular not to allow any statement of his to go unchallenged as he may be to challenge anything I say. So we might as well understand that just now.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I understand it.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I have as good authority for making the statements I have made as anyone can expect to have in this or any other country. If these wires to which I have referred are baseless then I must go back to those who sent them and tell them they are mistaken; also, if these newspaper reports are false, then we must advise the newspapers accordingly. But these are the authorities which I have, I have investigated them to the best of my ability, and I submit again that my statement in this regard is just as well founded as any statement which the minister has himself made.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend is very adroit at missing the point. He said these people were suffering. That is what I took exception to. Now he is slipping away from the suffering and dealing with dissatisfaction. I want my hon. friend to understand that he made a straight statement that these people were suffering, and I challenged that statement. I still challenge it and ask him to bring forward facts to show that anything of the kind has happened. Dissatisfaction is another matter altogether.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister himself has answered the question. He says I slip away from the point. I do not slip away from any point or any person. He says I charged that these men were suffering. Then he says they are not suffering, they are disappointed. Is not disappointment suffering? In the estimation of the minister can there be suffering more poignant than the disappointment of people who have come from their own land in response to appeals and promises, into what to them is a foreign country, only to find that they have been misinformed and befooled? Can anything be more keen than disappointment, or has the hon. minister no imagination? Can suffering not take place except someone sticks a pin into one or knocks one on the head? That is a crude concept of suffering. My conception covers a bigger
field. If you prove that these people have not suffered at all from want or cold, which has not been proven, there is no doubt that they have suffered and are still suffering in the keenest way from disappointment brought about by broken promises on the part of the government made in the name of the people in a new country. I conclude, Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I am veiy glad to
notice, Mr. Speaker, that the government and its supporters have taken my remarks so keenly, because it proves to me that I am hitting the nail on the head, or to change the analogy, am getting under their skins. I wish they would be as particular in the future about their own statements and about investigating matters as I have been in this particular case. And I hope that the enthusiasm which they display against anyone vho criticizes their policy will be switched into carrying their policy out in a positive manner. When that happens they will be doing a greater service to this country than they have yet accomplished, and we shall not have these people suffering as they are doing now. I say suffering, advisedly, Mr. Speaker, knowing that the mental suffering of these people is much keener than any physical suffering can possibly be. That is all I wish to say on the matter.

subsubtopic: ADJOURNMENT MOTION-MR. SPEARMAN-TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
In justice to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) who expressed a desire to reply, I would remind him that on a substantive motion only can a reply be made. If the hon. member will refer to paragraph 263 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms he will find the following definition of a substantive motion:
By a substantive motion is meant a motion not incidental to a proceeding before the House, and which can be dealt with by amendment or by the distinct vote of the House.
This motion for adjournment not being a substantive motion, a reply cannot be allowed. That is why I ruled out the hon. member.

On the first resolution:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg to mtove that the following resolution which appears as No. 44 on the order paper may be referred to the Committee of the Whole with the preceding resolution

Yes, wherever it

Amendment agreed to.

I have no objection.
I suppose, Mr. Chairman, that the object of this resolution is to give effect to the provincial legislation which has recently been enacted in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is what I was going to explain, Mr. Chairman.

I do not think there is any change in the salaries; it is simply carrying out the former intention as to what shall become of the two other divisions when the chiefs of those divisions no longer serve.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: By the last amendment passed by the legislature of Ontario iris provided that there shall be two appellate divisions and a high court division. The first appellate division will be presided over by the Chief Justice of Ontario, and there will be a second chief justice of the second division. When a vacancy occurs in the Exchequer Court or Court of Common Pleas the two judges now occupying those positions are not to be replaced. There will be a Chief Justice of the High Court, with the same number of judges. The judges of the Appellate Divisions will be known as Judges of Appeal. As my hon. friend has just suggested there is no increase in the number of judges and no increase in salaries.

This reduction is all right as far as it goes, but it does not go far enough. The province fixes the number of judges- and the Drury-Raney government kept many judges serving on their commissions. In the first place, there is a considerable decline in the litigation in Ontario in the High Court of Justice-a decline of from 25 to 30 per cent. The jurisdiction of the county courts has been greatly increased; fully 100 per cent; work that formerly was done by the High Court of Justice has been transferred to the county courts and the latter court is supplanting the High Court. In my opinion there are too many High Court judges in Ontario. Four of these judges were away the greater part of two years serving on Ontario government commissions-one of them on a purely political commission-going into the whole question of some $326,000,000 expended by municipalities on cheap light, power and radials. Two of these judges actually left their judicial duties to work on these political commissions-timber, hydro, radials and

Judges Act Amendment
other political matters-contrary to the statute passed by this House some years ago. Two of them left their duties for the greater part of two years, and, in the case of the two others, for a large portion of one year and a portion of another year respectively. Some of these judges can take holidays at any time, spring, summer, autumn or winter, to say nothing of the long vacation. While there are many good men, we have not on the bench to-day, on the average in Ontario, the men of ability that we had twenty-five years ago. I would point out that when a nation abounds in physicians it grows thin in people and when a nation abounds in judges and justices of the peace, as is the case in Ontario, especially in judges who can leave their judicial duties and go, as it were, on the political bench, then it becomes scarce in politicians. Some of these commission judges "toil not neither do they spin" at purely judicial court work. Now, as to the statute that was passed by the Union government in 1920, chapter 56, setting out an array of some 26 Ontario judges, I may say that no one was appointed who was a Conservative

everybody had to be Liberal to get an appointment from the Union goveTnment. I never belonged to the Union party myself, but one of the most extravagant pieces of legislation passed by the Union government was that same Judges Act of 1920, which is cited in the resolution, chapter 56 of the Statutes of Canada, 1920. Under that act there are three or four Chief Justices, some twenty-five High Court judges for Ontario, embracing a population of 2,500,000; in other words, Ontario has more or nearly as many High Court judges as the whole of England. If the present condition continues there will hardly be a lawyer in the province who is not also a judge. That will be like the condition that prevails in the United States, where practically every lawyer is a judge or is called judge and if he is not one to-day he hopes to be one tomorrow. I hope the minister will have a further survey made of this whole matter. I suggest that he inquire into the number of hours these judges sit, the number of holidays they take, the length of time they spend in giving attention to judicial duties and to political commissions, notwithstanding the statutes of 1920 by which in consideration of a raise in salary they were not to take these commissions. There is going to be an election in Ontario in a few days and we will not need next year a lot of these commission judges at all, because when they have abandoned their commissions there will be even less or nothing left for 230
them to do. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, Ontario has too many judges and there should be further co-ordination of judges there and a reduction could be made and a substantial economy effected. Judges should stick to their purely judicial work and keep out of political commissions to help this party and that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We cannot reduce
the number of judges in any province. The courts are created by the province and we provide the salaries of the judges; if any change is to be made in the number of judges, it must be done by the province. As to my hon. friend's allegation that some of the judges in Ontario have been acting on commissions connected with political matters, I do not see how that could be so, having regard to the amendment to which he has referred. It is true there was a proviso to cover investigations which had been started before the amendment was passed, but I do not see how any judge could subsequently act as my hon. friend has suggested without contravening the statute.
First resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The second resolution
is as follows:
Resolved, (1) That it is expedient to amend section seventeen of the Judges Act, as enacted by chapter thirty-eight of the statutes of 1914, and to provide that the salaries of the judges of the Circuit Court of the district of Montreal shall be as follows:-The senior judge of the said court, $8,000 per annum, and three other judges of the said court each $7,000 per annum; and to provide that the provisions of section ten of chapter fifty-six of the statutes of 1920 shall not apply to judges of the Circuit Court;
(2) That section two of the act to amend the Judges Act, chapter fifty-nine of the statutes of 1919, relating to the salaries of local judges in Admiralty, be repealed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Circuit Court
of Montreal is a division of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec; it is a special court for the district of Montreal. The jurisdiction which is given to these four judges represents a population of nearly a million people. In the other districts the administration of justice in the circuit jurisdiction is carried out by the judges of the Superior Court. The statistics show that in the district of Montreal these four judges have to decide more cases than all the judges of the Superior Court in the other districts. Their present salary is $5,500, and that of the Chief Justice is $6,000. We propose to give an increase of $1,500 to the three puisne judges and an increase of $2,000 to the Chief Justice. When the increase was given to the judges of the Superior Court in 1910 or 1911, these circuit court judges were so much re-

Judges Act Amendment

garded as judges of the Superior Court that it was assumed they would get the increase, and the result was that they were forgotten. They tried to have the error corrected later on, but they only obtained an increase of some $1,500. Since that time they have been asking that they be given proper treatment, and it is only after the receipt of resolutions from the bar of the province of Quebec and from the whole population of the district of Montreal that we bring down this resolution, which is, I think, only just, providing for a fair remuneration of these judges.
I take it from what my hon. friend says that the circuit court of Montreal is somewhat similar in its jurisdiction to the county courts of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, no.
What is the limit in the Ontario county court?

I was going to ask my hon. friend what the difference was. When I was practising the county court limit was $500, but that has been very greatly increased. I think now they can try practically anything under certain conditions. I think that is right, Mr. Chairman? You would be familiar with it being an active practitioner in the province.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
So that to-day under certain conditions they can try suits involving any amount no matter how big.
All appealable?
Oh yes, and I have no doubt that the decisions of the circuit court would be appealable.
Not to the amount of S100.

Anything as
small as that would be looked after in Ontario by the division court. In addition, the county courts in Ontario have a very large jurisdiction in criminal matters. The way matters are now conducted they have almost exclusive jurisdiction in criminal matters outside of murder and rape cases. I wpuld ask my hon. friend if he has statistics of the business done, for example, in Toronto on the one hand by the three judges-is it not?- that are working there and by the Montreal circuit judges on the other hand, and what are the salaries of the Toronto judges?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is a great
difference between the county court of On-
tario and the circuit court of Montreal. As I have said, this is a division of the Superior Court of the province just like a division of the Supreme Court of Ontario, and if it was not for the fact that we have four judges acting as judges of the circuit court of Montreal we would have to appoint four judges of the Superior Court to do the work. The circuit court is also a court of appeal.

It used to be ten years when I was at the bar.

There has alway.3 been a difference between the county court judges in Ontario and the circuit court judges in Montreal. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I said, there was an amendment passed in 1919 with respect to the judges in Admiralty which reads as follows:
"No salary shall be paid to any local judge in Admiralty of the Exchequer Court under the provisions of this section who is a judge of any provincial superior court, provided, that the provisions of this subsection shall not apply to any local judge in Admiralty who was or is appointed before the coming into force of this act.
In the province of Quebec we had Judge Lyman, I think-I do not remember the exact name- who was receiving an additional salar3' of $1,000. He died and was replaced by Judge Maclennan in 1920. Judge Maclennan, being deprived of that additional salary of $1,000, received fees under that ruling of the Exchequer Court and has been receiving them ever since. When we submitted certain amendments to the consideration of the House at the beginning of the present session seeking to amend the Admiralty Act we declared that in the future no judge should be allowed to receive fees. That bill is now before the Senate. It was represented, however, that we were not acting fairly to Judge Maclennan and the other judge I have mentioned, because they had been authorized by the previous administration to receive such fees and that if they were prohibited in the future from receiving fees they should be compensated in some other way. We cannot find any other
fSir Henry Drayton.]
means than the method we propose now of paying the judges of any supreme or superior court of the province this additional salary. I may say that all the judges who are acting as judges in admiralty were doing their ordinary work in a perfectly satisfactory manner. No reproach of any kind was made against them on any such ground, and I think we should allow them this additional remuneration.

My hon. friend did not catch the point I was making. 1 understand this will apply only to two gentlemen in the case of both of whom, certainly in the case of one, the appointment took place after the passage of the act to which the minister refers so that there is no right to this extra salary under that act. There was a clear intimation from parliament that there should not be any extra fee paid for that service, therefore, if special fees are accepted, I do not care how it was done, it is acting directly against the intent of that statute. In view of the bill which is before the Senate it seems to me the matter should stand just as it is, without that increase of $1,000, unless the minister thinks the statute of 1920 was entirely wrong. If the minister thinks the policy laid down by parliament was wrong well and good, but if he believes parliament was right when it said there should not be this extra salary I do not think the mere fact that these gentlemen were enabled to get fees in some other way should influence him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is special work of a judicial character. There is nothing in the amendment of 1919 *which said the judges would not be allowed to receive any fees It was after the appointment of Judge Maclennan that the Exchequer Court authorized the payment of fees to judges. This was known by the Minister of Justice and it was approved by the department. This has been going on now for nearly four years, and if we say that we are going to deprive these judges of these fees and tell them that they will have to act in future without remuneration of any kind I do not see how we can justify our position. The only remedy, it seems to me, is to revert to the old system and pay them an additional salary of $1,000.

I think the principle of permitting judges to act as arbitrators in railway matters is a very bad one. As everybody knows the railways are in politics all the time, and if we have judges acting as arbitrators in railway matters, we are going to have judges in politics, more or less, also. We had an illustration of the principle of this legislation in Ontario, where judges served on. arbitrations as to electric railway matters, and in assessing damages or compensation in these

matters. It was found by Sir Oliver Mowat to be a very bad principle. In arbitrations in regard to taking over electric lines, street railway plants or power and gas plants, in Ontario, experience proved that it was a very bad principle to have judges on these commissions, because appeals would have to be taken from the arbitration board in many cases on questions of fact, and also on questions of law, and some of the judges would sit in appeal in cases where they had acted as arbitrators. These arbitration judges will be looking for passes and all kinds of favours from the railways, and in civil cases against these same railways the judges should be in a position to be impartial. That view was corroborated the other night by the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales) when he asked me: How is it that people from the Old Land travelling in Canada never heard of the Canadian National Railways until they reached this country? He gave an instance of travelling a few weeks ago on the train and meeting people who had just come over and who had never heard of the Canadian National line. The president is very strong in the view that we ought to have some place in Paris to which every person goes and from which everybody who comes from the Continent emanates, as it were, the result being to enable the Canadian National system to secure its share of the immigration traffic as well as of the freight traffic; and I think he had this particular building in mind. However, some little time ago he received word that just the kind of building he required so far as location was concerned could be secured. He immediately wired to a gentleman in Paris to secure this building, as there were two or three other parties after it, and the Canadian National would temporarily finance it. If there was one thing that was always maintained by us it was this: That in connection with any matters which did not have to do with the direct administration of the company parliamentary control had to be there. It makes no difference whether the company honestly put up this two millions without any subterfuge or whether they put it up in this kind of a way. It is a matter of capital expenditure no matter for how short a period it is, and if the Minister of Finance is going to take the stand that that sort of thing can be done without his knowledge he is going to put himself in a very grave position. I do not think he approves of it; I am quite confident that on reflection he will not approve.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend think it is a good idea for the Canadian National Railways to have a continental headquarters in Paris?

It may or may not be good. It may be gross extravagance, or it may be of some use; I am not going to pass upon that question one way or the other. I can tell my hon. friend this, however: The statement made by the Minister of Railways that everything emanating from the Continent comes from Paris is entirely wrong.
I did not say so.
I understood my hon. friend to say so.
Not at all.

Then he did not say so. My hon. friend did not say this was the place from which everybody went or 
came; but the great bulk of the Continent's traffic I may tell him does not originate in Paris.
Most of it does, and the tourist traffic nearly all goes there.
I can well understand the desire of the Minister of Railways for tourist traffic. I suppose he is anticipating the fleets-to-be that he will have control of over the Atlantic.
No, I am having trouble with the fleets-that-are.
Take that statement as a test of his sincerity on this question of tourist business. Has he one passenger boat on his list that is equipped for tourist traffic?

I am sorry to report that my hon. friend, out of sixteen or seventeen steamers, did not build any capable of carrying passengers, but I do know that thousands of people cross the ocean on other steamships and have to take railway lines when they get here. They take railway lines when they are going across the continent to get to a steamship; and if, as has been the case in the past, there is nobody to sav "Canadian National" to them when they are coming over, they are not likely to taka the Canadian National when they get here.

Of course that all goes to show how completely the Minister of Railways has been overlooked by the president, and how absolutely he has been ignored, because if the president had taken him into his confidence-

Because it would not be arranged that way. It is arranged by running arrangements with steamship lines originating the traffic, and for the purpose of doing that it is not necessary to buy large premises like this. My hon. friend from Pictou wished to ask me a question.

speechtext: Does the hon. member say that if Sir Henry Thornton desired to build a branch line somewhere which he considered necessary for the business of the railway we should have nothing to say about it, and it should be done by the government ?

There is nothing strange about it We were supposed to have details of appropriation in connection with all these capital account matters. If the hon. gentleman thinks Sir Henry Thornton can do as he pleases in regard to the mileage of this system, he is entirely mistaken.

The hon.
member certainly said that he had nothing to do with capital expenditure.

The hon. member can gain nothing by puting words in my mouth. Sir Henry Thornton can do nothing in the way of capital expenditure without the consent of parliament. He has to go to the government and through the government to parliament, in order to get the vote. He makes his recommendations, of course, just as any other general manager makes his recommendations, to the gentlemen who provide the funds. There can be no doubt that this is a complete departure from the former practice, and what I want to know from the minister is whether he endorses in any way the doctrine of his colleague the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr Macdonald) and whether he thinks Sir Henry Thornton can build new lines without first coming to the government?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I never said that I thought Sir Henry Thornton could build new lines, without first coming to the government. My hon friend knows that perfectly well, and if he made the statement outside the House I would probably use language which is not parliamentary. But in the House I cannot say very much. My hon. friend took the ground that in regard to capital account the Minister of Railways was supreme under the act.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: He intimated that Sir Henry Thornton had no responsibility in regard to it. Does he mean to say the government can initiate these matters without the consent or recommendation of Sir Henry Thornton? My hon. friend is extremely misleading when he refers to what I said, but it is simply on a par with what he has been saying right along.

I thank my hon. friend for his clear, well-founded and beautiful statement. There is no mystery about it at all. What childishness to say the president has nothing to do with capital expenditure, when we at the same time say that he has to come to parliament to get authority for the capital expenditure? Would it not be childish to think that the government would initiate and go on with the work apart from the man they had paid to do it? The whole fact is that the onus is on the president. The president ought to make his recommendations just like any other manager or president, he makes them to the government and he cannot act on these of his own motion in connection with capital expenditure until the government say so and until parliament provides the money. There is no mystery about that at all-not the slightest. The whole trouble, Sir, is that we have to have a smoke screen erected, just simply in some way to becloud what is a very simple and clear matter. Here is $2,000,000 taken, so far as parliament knows, merely to assist in a land speculation, out of which some unknown syndicate may or may not be making money, and we cannot even know who compose the syndicate. My hon. friend said that a fair rent was to be paid, and he is to have just as much area as he wants. What is the rent to be paid per foot?

My hon. friend is not as dense as he pretends to be; I do him the honour to believe that he understood what I said. Every man in the House knows what I said, and if there is any hon. gentleman here who should not say anything at all about one man putting words into the mouth of another it is the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). I never before, in the short space of thirty minutes, had what I said twisted on the one hand and remain unheeded on the other as I have just experienced in the past half hour. I told the hon. gentleman distinctly that the transaction had not yet been completed but that the Canadian National Railways, in this way, had secured a home where it was needed in the best part of Paris. I made it clear that it could secure all the space it required at what was decided upon as a fair rental.
Who is to decide what is a fair rental?
I suppose that every bargain is made between two parties. If my hon. friend were going to rent floor space from me he would not ask parliament to decide what that space should be.

Then the bargain, I gather, is not yet made. If what the hon. gentleman says is correct, it appears that the bargain has not yet been consummated. I want to know whether or not it has been made. If it has already been made, then the rental is certain. The committee wants to know7 how the matter stands.

There my hon. friend goes again, endeavouring to twist what I said and to interject into it something that may make it appear what it is not. I told him the details had not yet been concluded but that the Canadian National Railways would have a home at a fair rental decided upon between two men w7ho understand the business.

I gather from what the minister says that t'he situation is somewhat in this position. The representative of the Canadian National Railways in Paris, that is to say, a regularly paid official of the railways, secured an option of space in a property in Paris. The Canadian National Railway Company has pledged itself to the vendors to the extent of $2,000,000 on behalf of an unknown syndicate, the names of whose members are not divulged to the House. This transaction, involving a committal of $2,000,000 of capital expenditure on the part of the railways, was launched without the knowledge of the government and before they were aware that it was being done. I think I am justified in assuming that Sir Henry Thornton, as President of the National Railways, undertook that transaction on his own responsibility. When it became known to the public of this country a week or two ago there certainly was reflected in the press and through other media a very severe criticism of the action in expending $2,000,000 for quarters in Paris, and then, as an afterthought, apparently, this syndicate came into existence. I do not assert that as a fact, but it undoubtedly is a fair inference to draw from the very meagre information we have been accorded. Now, the minister says that we are committed to $2,000,000; and we do not know whether this syndicate possesses the wherewithal to pay for that money for which we have stood responsible. Certainly, up to the present it has not undertaken to pay. So that we have committed ourselves to this sum of money; we have in a sense committed ourselves, as a country, to a bargain to rent space in this hotel building.
Not as a country.

Well, the company acting on behalf of the government, because it is a

capital expenditure. We must differentiate in that regard; the expenditure is not a current one.
I do not agree with the hon. member.

Will the minister be good enough to lay on the Table such documents as may exist, upon which this 32,000,000 was advanced? I cannot conceive that even Sir Henry Thornton would authorize an advance of such a sum of money without some form of documentary agreement or understanding. I do not wholly agree with the minister in his refusal to divulge the names of those who comprise the syndicate. This is a very different matter from divulging current detail business. Here is a syndicate of gentlemen, New Yorkers, apparently, who are securing a property in Paris, said to be of very excellent value, for $2,000,000. We, the people of Canada, are putting up the money for the time being. That is not the type of transaction that justifies secrecy or concealment, even temporarily, for the sake of confidence. Surely we ought to know who the members of this syndicate are. I say, I do not agree with the minister in his refusal to give their names; I think it would inspire a great deal more confidence in the whole transaction if they were revealed.
I would ask the minister, first, to give to the committee all the details of the arrangement upon which this advance of $2,000,000 is based, because that is a reasonable request; and I again point out that it is capital expenditure and not a matter of current business, which I fully agree with him should not necessarily be divulged. Business of a current character I do not say ought to be revealed; but this is not such business; this is a matter of capital expenditure,
9 p.m. just as if we undertook to build a piece of railway or to construct a building in some of our holdings in the United States or in any other part of the world. It is a straight capital expenditure, and I submit that the committee is entitled to full information. Let me fortify that opinion. In the very item under discussion, the details in regard to which we shall request of the minister, there is a reference to operating deficits, acquisition of property and materials and supplies. Under that head I asked the minister a little while ago whether this matter was included, and he said it was not. But he has every detail before him which he will divulge to parliament and upon which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will make an advance of $73,000,000. That
is where the former Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is right in his protest, and it will not answer the question for the minister to say that the law passed under the leadership of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) in 1919 provided for all this. The law did not provide for this or any similar transaction at all; it provided exactly against such transactions.
Referring briefly to the suggestions made by the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), I want to assure the committee that we are not seeking to interfere with the management of the railways. No; we are seeking to bring that management to account for departing from the clear intent of the law in this matter in making a capital commitment of $2,000,000 without even the knowledge of the minister. That is our point.

I am glad my hon. friend puts it that way. I asked the ex-Minister of Finance distinctly, and he was careful not to say that the transaction was contrary to the act. Now, this transaction was approved in the first place by the financial department of the Canadian National Railways, and afterwards by Mr. Ruel, whose knowledge of these matters will, I think, be conceded to be equal to that of any other legal authority in this country. So it is out of the question to find fault with the president and his board of directors. They take Mr. Ruel's legal opinion, and up to date it has been found to be sound. He thoroughly approves the legality of this transaction. My hon. friend insists that we purchased the building. We did not.

I say the government is
committed to a capital expenditure of $2,000,000 for the purchase of a building.

It is not committed to a capital expenditure. It has financially backed a man who has bought this building, which is to be transferred. The Canadian National Railway simply became responsible for the financing of the project temporarily, and temporarily only.

Permit me to interrupt.
But this commitment of $2,000,000 is on the say-so of a paid official of the National Railways-the Paris representative. Now, that man has no responsibility whatever. We might as well have had a clerk out of the department. The only difference, perhaps, would have been in their respective status, that is all.

Mr. Chairman, we are
asked to vote $73,000,000 for this particular

item, or twice the expenditure of all Canada's *estimates in 1894. When the budget was introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) he told us that but for the railway *deficits we could have had some reduction in taxation. These railways deficits are bearing very heavily on the people to-day, and in my opinion the vote should not be passed until it has been reported upon by the Railway Commission. A royal commission composed of Mr. A. H. Smith, Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Acworth investigated our railways in 1917, and the most important part of their report was that in which they dealt with the subject of capital expenditure. They recommended, in effect, that before such a vote as this was passed there should be a report on it by some responsible body appointed by parliament for that particular purpose. Mr. Smith, then president of the New York Central, recommended, and Sir Henry Drayton, then chairman of our Railway Commission, agreed with him, that we should:
Amend the regulating policy so that the Railway 'Commission may have jurisdiction over all railroads in the matter of maximum and minimum rates, the issuance of securities, the building of new railways, or the extension of lines, and other matters properly [DOT]within the scope of governmental supervision.
The National Railway Board are committing the country to capital outlays running into millions of dollars, and we may well ask ourselves to-night: Have we responsible government in Canada? The board visited the city of Ottawa recently, looked over the terminals and then anounced that millions of dollars would be spent on their improvement. They proceeded to the city of Hamilton, *where after inspecting the National Railways' facilities there they announced further expenditures of millions of dollars. Then they came to the city of Toronto and arranged to erect a sky-scraper office building. All this was done without consulting the government or parliament. Last year a vote for a similar purpose went through very easily and large sums of money were provided for the physical improvement of these railway properties, for their co-ordination, for additional rolling stock and for certain branch line construction. But after the expenditure of all that money what do we find? It was hoped some coordination would be effected, but very little has been done towards this end. True, the railways have not done badly during the past year, but the point is that we should scrutinize these expenditures a little more carefully at the time we vote them and not wait until recess to find out what we do about them.

But notwithstanding this large capital outlay what do we find in the annual report of the Canadian National Railways which was laid on the table a few weeks ago? We find that the gross earnings decreased by nearly $7,000,000, the figures for 1921 being $127,000,000 as against $120,135,000 for 1922. The operating expenses in 1921 were in round figures $143,000,000 as against $129,000,000 in 1922, or a reduction of $14,000,000-not so bad. There was also a reduction of abo>-$7,000,000 in the operating deficit, the figures being $16,000,000 for 1921 as against $9,000,000 for 1922. These again are round figures. Some betterments were made, but they were not of a character to increase the earnings, and it would be far better for the directors to bear this in mind when making further capital outlay. The new station in Toronto is still standing idle	waiting	the building	of	theviaduct, and these increased facilities alone would, I believe, augment the earnings in that district by at least one-third. The annual National Railway report states that the decrease in passenger traffic is discouraging, particularly as the quality of the service given has improved and because the rate for passenger travel in Canada is relatively low, being generally slightly below the prevailing rates in the	United	States. This	is	notstrictly accurate, for in the United States they have special holiday, week end	andexcursion rates, which we do not now enjoy to as	great	an extent.	In	the
freight earnings there is a loss of revenue due to the Crowsnest pass agreement rates, estimated to be six and a half mill .on dollars. The freight, passenger and express earnings were all less than in 1921. A hundred and seventy miles of new road were put into operation in the past twelve months in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. I do not criticize the board for that at all, I have no doubt it was necessary, but large sums of money were spent on betterments from which they do not get any revenue. The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman) pointed out last year that $50,000 to $75,000 per day can be saved in railway expenses by up-to-date co-ordination. Have we got that co-ordination to-day? We have not. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) pointed out recently that in his own city there are no signs of co-ordination, that trains are running on parallel lines so close together that they are within a stone's throw of each other. The same thing may be seen on the north shore of Lake Ontario, and the trains running between Toronto, Whitby and

Supply-R ailways-C.N.R.
Belleville could in my opinion be co-ordinated and a large saving effected.
I think the Canadian National Railway Board has altogether too much /power-a power that is prejudicial to our system of responsible government. I believe that the Canadian National Railway Board should have a free hand to administer the railway system; there should be no political interference whatsoever. The government of the country has proceeded along proper lines in this respect during the last few years. The present ministry has been more than sympathetic and has been doing very good work as far as it has gone, but there has not been the co-ordination that there should be. The present head of this railway has been going up and down the country making speeches and promising sidings, lines, terminals, skyscrapers, here, there and everywhere. Now, one of the most important feeders of the National Railways should be the merchant marine, on the ocean, on the river St. Lawrpnce, and on the Great Lakes. What has made the Canadian Pacific the great railway it is today, with its large earning power per mile? It has been very largely the co-ordination which has existed between its ocean and lake services and its rail communications. So our National Railways might very well take a leaf out of its rival's book, instead of recommending the sale of that merchant marine, constituting, as it does, an important feeder to the railway line. Now, I say that something should be done to bring our National Railways up to date. I would like to mention one or two matters in connection with which economies might well be effected. I have seen members travelling on the trains, and I have seen a large number of private cars proceeding all over the country. I knew a gentleman connected with the railway offices who used to have an office position in Toronto; there are big officials of that kind who could not go as far as Hamilton without dragging a private car along the right of way, even with coal as high as from $10 to $15 a ton. And in other ways there has not been co-ordination. There have been transfers of officials from Moncton to Montreal, from one city to another, and so far as I know there has not been any economy effected by the transfer. So I say that co-ordination has not been effected and economies have not been brought about which would increase the efficiency of the system.
There is another branch of the administration of this railway system which must receive attention if success is to be attained; every employee must be satisfied, must be
happy and contented. That condition doe3 not prevail to-day on the National Railways. As I say, the minister is doing the best he can; he has done very good work, but in my opinion the principle of promotion should apply on this line as it does on the New York Central, Michigan Central, the Baltimore and Ohio, and on the Pennsylvania and Lake Shore lines. An announcement was made the other day from the general offices of the Baltimore and Ohio Railway that the principle of promotion would apply to all its employees from the very bottom of the ladder to the top, even to the presidency of that great railway. The same principle applies on the Pennsylvania lines and on the New York Central lines. But what have we in Canada? We are sending to England and to the United States for people to take high positions ir connection with our railway system; although there is an alien labour law, as I understand it, on the statute book to-day, people are being brought in here to take positions that ought to go to Canadians. I say that the principle of promotion is the best, principle; it is the principle which applies on all the leading railway systems of the United States and England. The leading railway officials in these countries have come from the ranks; the best men we have on our railways in this country have come from the ranks. I do hope that this principle will not be forgotten in the future.
Certain regional areas have been established by the present board of directors of the National Railway system. That was a very popular phrase with Julius Caesar-"regions Caesar never knew," and so on. It is a very high-sounding term, "regional area," but I cannot see where any needed co-ordination or economies are effected as the result of the establishment of these regional areas.
As to rates, there has been some downward trend. In that connection I wish to point out that by legislation of last session provision was made for certain additional rolling stock. During the last twelve months there have been added to the equipment 870 new freight cars, 561 additional freight cars, 26 passenger cars. With all these 1,600 new freight cars and the others that they had on hand a year ago, there are three months in the year when these cars are standing idle, although they could be transporting coal and other products from the prairie provinces to the head of the lakes and to central Canada. A rate of $9 a ton has been quoted on coal. I submit that the earnings of the road could be very largely increased and this $73,000,000 item could be very much reduced if instead

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

of allowing a large number of old and new cars to stand idle during three or four months of the year they were utilized to bring down the products I have named from Alberta to central Canada. During the first year or two of these operations there might be a deficit, but I am confident that as the years went on a surplus would result.
The present charges against the railways ere as follows:	construction, $587,000,000,
equipment, $88,000,000; deficit, $122,000,000; fixed charges, $145,000,000. These figures are almost appalling. Unless new sources of revenue are devised, these enormous charges e.re going to mean increased taxation on the people of Canada for many years to come, under the present system of operation of our National Railways.
Now, some hon. gentlemen sitting in this chamber have blamed public ownership for these deficits. But public ownership is not responsible; it is private ownership that has been responsible for the mismanagement of our railways. Public ownership did not build the Canadian Northern. Public ownership did not build the Grand Trunk. Public ownership did not build the Grand Trunk Pacific or the National Railways. These railways were built under private auspices and we now have these appalling deficits. So I say that the members of the committee should examine very carefully this item of $73,000,000. In my opinion, many of the capital expenditures that have been made during the past twelve months might easily have waited over-many of the so-called betterments, the erection of sidings and terminals, the building of 73 new stations, and so on, many of them in districts that are not self-sustaining. The people of Ontario are behind the National Railways; they are doing everything they can to support the publicly-owned system. In the district from which I come, 326 cities in the hydroelectric movement have had for some time past a working arrangement with the National Railways, designed to promote the interests of that particular system, and they intend to continue it. Everybody wants to give the National Railways a chance. But the minister mentioned the other day one reason why the head of our National Railways system should become a member of the board of Canada Steamships. Now, it was brought out in the lake freights inquiry that the railways of Canada fixed the rates on the lakes for waterborne traffic. That is stated in the report; I need not read it. If there is one thing more than another that is going to help to eliminate the deficit on the Canadian National Railways it is the advantage that

waterborne traffic will give on lake, river and ocean as a feeder of our National Railways. I am very much disappointed, as a believer in the national system, that the head of the system has joined the board of Canada Steamships, which has a monopoly' on the Great Lakes to-day, as is set out in the report to which I have referred. Now, the reason the minister gave for the president of the system becoming a member of that board was that there was an exchange of traffic between the National Railways and Canada Steamships. Well, there is also an exchange of traffic with the Canadian Pacific, with the New York Central, with the Michigan Central; is it proposed to offer the same argument in that connection, namely, that for that reason Sir Henry Thornton should become a director of the Canadian Pacific, of the New York Central, of the Michigan Central? I do not think that argument could reasonably be offered. The president of the National Railways may be a many-sided man, but he can-Dot serve two masters; he cannot serve Canada Steamships and the National Railways as well.
The minister presented a very excellent annual statement at Easter with regard to the Canadian National Railways. I believe the day is not far distant when the onerous burden on the Finance Minister, the Minister of Railways, and the people of Canada in respect of our railways will be relieved. I believe a better day is dawning for our national system under public ownership. I believe that a united effort should be made in support of the National Railways. Municipalities and every patriotic citizen who has the welfare of this country at heart should work in harmony with the directors of the railways and the government should do all possible to see if something cannot be done to eliminate the deficits.
In my opinion this vote of $73,000,000 should be cut in two. I do not believe there is any need of spending $73,000,000 of the people's money for betterments on this railway in view of the deficits that have to be made up from year to year. I believe that if there was more co-ordination there would be less deficits. The acquisition of new property can wait till the railway is in a better position. Why should we build sky scrapers when we cannot get a proper terminal in a city of 500,000 people? I do not think the committee would be justified in voting this amount of money, a large amount of which is to be spent on betterments, construction and rolling stock. In my opinion the money on a lot of these betterments to the railway will have no earning power for many years to come. Furthermore, there is no line

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
in America, that is spending such a large amount of money on betterments and equipment, and the National is supposed to be a new system, with new rolling stock, new stations, and so forth. I think in view of the expenditure of some $587,000,000 to date on capital, as I pointed out before, on the National Railways, we could get along for a while without new branch lines, sidings and turn-outs, and call a halt on a lot of it that is not immediately revenue producing.
I believe it was wrong on the part of the new Railway Board to countermand the nopolitics order. I believe that no good will come from the revocation of that order by the chairman of the board after he had been in office only a short time and had had only a cursory look over the system. I have here the report of the Royal Commission on Railways of 1917 which recommends against the employees of the system being allowed to take part in politics. In May, 1903, there was another royal commission on transportation appointed in Canada which also recommended the same thing. They have had the same experience in the United States, and in Victoria, Australia, where the men went on strike and alienated public sympathy by their attitude in 1903. I think the no politics order was right and proper, and showed the wisdom of Mr. Hanna, and now the new directorate is turning things topsy-turvy and upsetting the nopolitics order. I say that is not even in the interests of the men because under public onwership the men need never be afraid of their employers. They will be better treated than under private employers. Their employers can afford to pay because the railway is operating at cost.
In conclusion, I wish the National Railways every success. I believe that before many days are over this magnificent investment of the people of Canada will be able to pay its way. It is a magnificent system, one of the largest and one of the best conducted in the world. We had no strikes on the railway last year. The passenger service in Ontario has never been equalled. So much is that the case that the National Railway is taking business from the Canadian Pacific on all the main lines in Ontario. If we can only do something to keep down the expenses, if we can complete the deepening of the Welland canal and encourage water-borne traffic as a feeder to the Nationals, I believe that a day of prosperity lies before the National Railways.

I listened with great interest to the remarks made by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). I wish to say very frankly that I was astonished to hear my hon. friend express surprise

In the first place I am going to take up what was said by the Acting Minister of National Defence. However, I will take my share of the responsibility although I was not here when this legislation was enacted. Now, the question of new lines is dealt with by section 23 of the Act to Incorporate the National Railway Company which provides:
With the approval of the Governor in Council and upon any location sanctioned by the Minister of Railways and Canals-
The committee will see two checks there. The first is that the minister has to pass upon this capital expenditure, and afterwards the Governor in Council has to do the same thing.
-the company may from time to time construct and operate railway lines, branches and extensions, or railway facilities or properties of any description in respect to the construction whereof respectively, parliament may hereafter authorize the necessary expenditure, or the guarantee of an issue of the company's securities. A copy of any plan or profile made in respect of any completed railway shall be deposited with the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada.
Hon. gentlemen will see that we have here a thorough and most complete check, the check of parliament. These lines can only be built either b3^ money voted by parliament, or else guaranteed by parliament, so that we have a complete check through parliament, the department, and the Governor in Council on these capital expenditures. The thing is so clear I am not quite sure that the Acting Minister of National Defence, seeing the necessity of a smoke screen of some kind, did not utter the first thing that came into his head. He really could not have considered the submission he was making. That is all I wish to refer to, because the thing is very clear.
Now I invite the attention of the hon. member for Dorchester to my next point. The position of the directors of this road is the same as the position of the directors of an ordinary railway company. I think my hon. friend will agree with that. It has not advanced beyond that point. Then, Mr. Chairman, I want to point out that there is a substitution of the shareholders under the act for the Governor in Council. The people of Canada are thp shareholders, represented by the Governor in Council, in so far as powers under the act to be exercised by shareholders are concerned. My hon. friend will find that section 9 of the act of 1919, chapter 13, makes that absolutely clear. It reads:
When, under the provisions of the Railway Act or any other statute or law, the approval, sanction or confirmation by shareholders is required, such approval, sanction or confirmation may be given by the Governor in Council.
So that the committee will see that what has been done under this act is very plain. The directors have the right to carry on business just exactly in the same way as the directors of any other railway company have, and for the shareholders their powers, votes and meetings is substituted the action or the consideration of the Governor in Council. The thing is perfectly clear, therefore. I need not elaborate the point with my hon. friend for Dorchester. He would not for one moment contend, I take it, under the provisions of the Railway Act, that directors can enter new fields, and hazard the capital of the company in new ventures, without the assent of the shareholders. I think we would all have to admit that. Then if that be the case, the position is1 the same, so far as this board is concerned. They cannot enter new fields and they cannot risk the country's money without the government, acting for the shareholders, assenting. I take it we can have no dispute down to that point. So that the whole result is that these directors have no greater powers than any other directors. They are just in the same position.

They have just as much
power.

Just as much, but no more, and if my friend will consult the legal members around him, I think they will agree that that is absolutely correct. The proposition then is that these -directors can do the same as any other directors. The Canadian National never entered the continental field at any time. They had no offices over there of any kind. I am not saying this for the purpose of trying the matter out. No one would call to order directors who entered into a lease for the purpose of trying the matter out with small commitments-commitments that should be made out of the year's business. That would be all right, but that is not what we have. We have an entry into a new field, plus the application of the moneys which ought, under the act, to have been applied in the discharge of the regular obligations of the company, to a purpose entirely new and outside the former operations of the company. That would not be illegal if you had the shareholders say so-I admit that. its basement was to be used for moving pictures to encourage immigration from France to Canada. It struck me at that time that we had never had a large immigration from Fiance. In the first place France does not encourage emigration, and in the second place Canada has not apparently attracted the French people of recent years. I made it my business while we were discussing this to look up the statistics of immigration to Canada from other countries, and I find a number of countries from which we get a very much larger immigration than France. So if there is any reason for having this large building in Paris from the immigration standpoint, and that was the point emphasized in the press, there is a very much greater reason for having such a building in some of these other countries. The figures here are from 1909 to 1915, and I find that the immigration from Scotland before the war, and it is perhaps better to take those figures than the figures of to-day, was between five and ten times greater than the immigration from France. The immigration from Austria was more before the war than the immigration from France, the same is true of Germany, and in a greater degree still of Russia; it is true of Italy, and from little Sweden even if we received as many immigrants as from France. Then in regard to imports and exports the same holds true, although the figures vary for the different countries. Switzerland exports to Canada much more heavily than France, and the other countries I mentioned receive a much greater amount of imports from Canada than France. Therefore it appears to me that it would be necessary in some of these other countries from which we get a greater number of people and with which we do a greater trade than with France to have some building of that sort. It may be answered that Sir Henry Thornton should be more familiar with the matter than I am, and of course he is, but it struck me in looking over these figures that we are doing more business with some of these other countries and receiving a much larger immigration from them. I just wished to point that out. Certainly it would appear to the ordinary observer that this is a case of policy. It is not a case of ordinary expenditure. I admit that we have no right to interfere, I do not think the government should interfere in the ordinary management of the railways, and I believe that all members in this corner of the House will take that view, but in the ordinary expenditure of capital, and this is an ordinary expenditure of capital, it is a question of policy, and before a question of policy

There is another matter coming under the head of what I would call extraordinary expenditure. In the press some days ago it was stated that the Canadian Pacific in conjunction with the Canadian National Railways were granting $100,000 yearly for a period of five years to the Canada Colonization scheme. Now in view of the very long discussion we had on immigration when those estimates were before the House does the minister approve of this plan? Is it true that the Canadian National Railways have made such a grant? So far as I am concerned I am not against any company bringing people into this country, but I was wondering whether the minister or the department approved of this grant for that purpose.

I am not sure that it has been discussed so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned. I want to say again that the Canadian National Railway Board run their business under the provisions of the act, I do not think they have entered into the arrangement as yet, but if they had done so it would certainly be after full consideration, in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway-these being the two greatest transportation companies-and for the purpose of bringing settlers into Canada. Speaking from the Canadian National standpoint-yes, speaking from the national standpoint-I think the salvation of Canada is to get more people of the right kind into this country. I think that is true, and anything that would tend to that end would, I think, have the approval of parliament. As to the particulars in this case I am not conversant with them to a greater extent than I have already informed my hon. friend.
You say then that you think it would be a profitable arrangement for this country?
If properly administered I would think so.

I have been waiting for a couple of hours now in the hope that I and the committee might obtain some definite information in regard to the question of the purchase of the hotel site in Paris for the National Railway system, and I am sorry to say that after having listened for that period of time I know as little about the subject now as I did when the discussion started. There is this to be said, however, that I think the minister himself knows very little about the transaction. No member of the government knows more than the Minister of Railways about this matter, and if his information upon it is nil the information of the government is likewise nil, and up to the present time the information of the committee is nil also. Now what is the position? I may say it is a serious one. I realize that the Minister of Railways has for two hours to-night treated the matter with the greatest jocularity. It may be his natural good humour but he has certainly tried rather to make a joke of the idea-
Not at all.

-that the House or the country is entitled to any information in regard to this subject upon which there is considerable public discussion, perhaps some little public misapprehension, and perhaps some little public curiosity because of the payment of $2,000,000 of the money of the people of this country in the manner in which it has been done in this instance, from the facts disclosed. The whole of the circumstances regarding the withdrawal of that money from the treasury of the National Railway Company are so shrouded in mystery as to raise some curiosity and anxiety in the public mind; and I thihk that the government and the minister would do well to reconsider the position they have taken upon this question to-night. I do not suppose the public will be satisfied with the statement made by the minister; I believe that from one end of Canada to the other it will be found that there is a reasonable and a general demand that fuller information than we have as yet received be given, and be given now and not postponed until it is too late for any purpose. If a system is growing up under the act or under the railway practice of this country whereby the president of a railway system-even

What an anomaly it is, what a strange thing it is, what a mysterious thing it is, that this syndicate of New Yorkers should get Sir Henry Thornton to go to the treasury of the Canadian National Railways for $2,000,000 to pay to a bank-I do not know whether it is a New York bank or a Canadian bank, I do not know what bank it is-and pull the chestnuts out of the fire for them.
That is not the situation at all.
That is the way I gleaned (he facts from the discussion that has taken place to-night.
You have been listening to the speeches of the gentlemen beside you, not to mine.

I have been listening to the speeches made in this committee, and if I am wrong in what I say the minister should be the last one to complain, because he has given us no facts whatever upon which to base a correct statement. Is it the law, or is it the practice to-day, that Sir Henry Thornton is entitled to use that amount of money to purchase a site in Paris, or in London, or anywhere else? If he can do that, if that is good practice, if that system is to be permitted, to-morrow he can take $10,000,000 out of the company's treasury and finance a

New York corporation in the purchase of a building on Wall street. It would be possible for him to take another $10,000,000 and spend it in New York. Why, it is in the power of the president to ruin the country, absolutely to ruin it, carrying the principle to its logical conclusion. I submit the principle is wrong. I submit the principle is illegal. I submit the practice ought not to exist; and if the minister, or the government, or parliament, has any control the system will be put an end to at the earliest possible moment.
Is it any wonder that the people and the press of Canada are a little curious upon this question? A capital expenditure of $2,000,000 by the National Railway Board, with a huge annual deficit, is something to stagger the public of any country. Now we have this
S2,000,000 added to that deficit, then another million and a quarter is taken for the purpose of purchasing a block on a street corner in the city of Toronto which, with all deference, I submit was not an immediately necessary expenditure at all, thus adding still more to our deficit. Is it any wonder, in view' of these facts, that the people are curious, that they desire more definite information than they have been able to get.
I have never, in all my experience, seen a minister of the Crown stand up in this House and try to justify an expenditure of $2,000,000 and make the statement practically, "I know nothing about it. I know there is a syndicate, but I do not even know their names. I know the money was taken out of the National Railway treasury to assist the syndicate in the financing of this purchase." That is the position of the minister to-night, and that absolute non-disclosure of material facts, that refusal to give us agreements or information -without advancing any real reason for such refusal except the statement that it will be detrimental to the interests of the National Railways-is a bold, bald statement. It is not a reason, it is an ipse dixit of the minister. Of course, we may not be able to get anything more, but I think he might take us into his confidence and say what it is would be so detrimental to the public interest if he gave us a reasonable disclosure of the leading facts in regard to this transaction.
One effect of such a statement would be to restore some public confidence in the road and in its management. An immediate effect would be to allay a great deal of public curiosity. It will not go down with the people, and will not satisfy the House, to say that Gerald Ruel, counsel for the railroad, advised Sir Henry Thornton, and Sir Henry Thornton advised me, and all I, as Minister

He was pressed for particulars and that was his answer. He would not have given that answer if he had not been pressed. I am pointing out his weakness and his great indignation. I understand it all. He has tried it for fifteen or twenty minutes and cannot do it. He has tried by, I will not say wilful misrepresentation, but he has said that I have not given the facts to the House. I would take Mr. Ruel's advice on these railway matters as quickly as I would
take his advice, and so would the president. He is paid to give that advice. So far as Mr. Ruel's advice is concerned, anything that was done by the president was within the four corners of the act.
