I did not say a lot of things that he mentioned, but I did say a lot of things he has not mentioned. Hansard will show all that. I have given a straightforward statement of the transaction, as given me by the board of directors. I might not have done all these things, if I had been president, but I am not president. The president did these things and Mr. Ruel, his adviser, said these things were done legally. I am not arguing,, and I have not argued, that I would have done these things in this way, or that my hon. friend would have done these things; but I did say the president got legal advice, and I trust the arrangement will be beneficial to the Canadian National.

If the minister's
interpretation of the act is correct, it seems to me that we are drifting into a most extraordinary and dangerous situation in Canada. I suppose very few of us have realized the implications of the Railway Act. Probably because of the unfortunate experience of the past years, we have been so much afraid of having politics brought into our railways that we have gone to the other extreme. The Canadian people have been willing to grant a good deal of power to outside commissions or boards in the hope that these outside commissions or boards would be able to carry on the affairs of the country more efficiently when freed from the nagging of individual members of the House. At the same time, we must not lose sight of the fact that the Canadian people, through their representatives in this House, are responsible for the expenditures of public money. That is the big thing. If we are to erect a board or commission that is practically free from effective criticism, then we have come to a very dangerous pass in our history. The people of this country-at least I can speak for the people of western Canada

have been tremendously interested in this Canadian National Railway system and the whole scheme of public ownership. Yet we are beginning to discover that, after all, the only

thing that is national in this railway is the name, and, perhaps, I should add, the deficits. The bondholders are very largely the financial beneficiaries of this road. They seem to be secure. The losses are borne by the people of Canada. We must remember too that in its organization the railways do not come at all closely under the direction of our Canadian people. The management is not at all democratic in its character.
I should like to mention in passing the position that has been taken again and again by Labour, that the employees should be directly represented on these public boards. I believe that the liberal party gave assurances that the employees would be represented on the board of management. The employees are not represented. Years have passed, and we see no indication-

I think the hon. member will recollect that the Prime Minister's suggestion was that Labour would be represented. Labour is represented by one of the ablest labour men on this continent-Tom Moore. He was one of the first men put on the board.

I think I remember when that matter was up for discussion some little time ago, that the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) pointed out very clearly that the promise was that rhe employees would be represented, and I submit that the appointment of a particular labour man, however estimable he may be, does not in any way make him in the sense in which we understand it in democratic countries a representative of Labour. The claim is, and has been throughout, that the employees themselves, those who work on the road would have some share in the management of the affairs of the road. That is not the case to-day. Further there seems to be no effective way in which the people of this country through their representatives can control the policies of this board. I think we had it some time ago from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that if there came a time of strain, undoubtedly the policies of the board would have to be regulated by the people of this country. I suggest that when these enormous deficits are piling up and the people are being asked to meet them, the time has already come when we should have a larger voice in the determination of the policies of the railroads.
It is all very well to say that we should keep clear of politics in regard to these matters. Yet I submit that after all politics is simply the business of the country, and a 
great corporation of this kind cannot possibly carry on its affairs without being in touch with the politics or with the business of the country at a score of different points. We' find that already the president of this railway has been associated with the presidents of other railways in what might very well be termed a transportation trust-a serious thing when we consider that the primary object of having a Canadian National road is that we may serve the people. This great trust or monopoly is operating, not primarily in the interests of the people but above all thing3 in the interests of the corporations. We are told again and again that our Canadian National Railways constitute an independent corporation which should be able to carry on business in its own way. I submit that if we allow this enterprise to be carried on in such a way we shall be no better off than we should be if the Canadian National Railways were a private concern. Here, for instance, is a question that arises in connection with this particular transaction involving $2,000,000. We are informed that it is desirable that we should encourage tourist traffic. I want to speak in behalf of a great many people of this country and to declare that there are other things a great deal more important to Canada than the encouragement of tourist traffic. There are a great many more important matters that require our consideration. I will not say that possibly tourist traffic might not be advantageous to the railways as a side-line. That might be the case. But I do say that if we intend to enter upon a new policy, or develop a policy, in that direction, we should not do so without that policy being decided upon in this House. That is the point that should be emphasized.
Could the hon. member tell me of one practical railwayman in this House who could advise along those lines?

There is something a great deal more needed to-day than the advice of practical railway men; and I,am not decrying for a moment the advice that they can give. But when we are asked to vote tens of millions of dollars of a deficit, then I say that the people who are being asked to supply that money, are essentially the people who should decide the policies. It is all very well to have experts come in and advise upon certain policies and carry them out; but there are larger affairs that ought to be determined by the people, and by the people alone. I might suggest to the hon. gentleman who asked me the question that there are no practical engineers in this

House; at least I presume not. If we required a bridge built we would need an expert to advise us on the matter; but there is the fundamental question as to whether or not we want the bridge built. We are in the position of those who have to decide, since presumably we are speaking on behalf of the people, and are voting these moneys for them.
The same thing is true with regard to the immigration policy. We are placed in a very absurd position indeed in this respect. We spend days and even weeks discussing the immigration policy of Canada, discussing the question whether or not we shall have more immigrants come into the country, and then we find that we are paying tens, almost hundreds of millions of dollars to a corporation which is running things for its own ends, by its own methods, with the object of bringing people into the country. It is preposterous that, should we decide that we do not want immigrants to come into Canada, a corporation independent of parliament can institute a policy that will bring us immigrants by tens or hundreds of thousands. I repeat, it is an absurd situation. This is manifest surely in the response of the Minister of Railways to the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) with regard to this item of $500,000 which is to be granted during five years-at least the suggestion was that it should be granted for five years-to the Canadian Colonization Company. We have held up this House for hours discussing items of less than $100,000; and yet here is a matter involving, over five years, an expenditure of $500,000, to promote a definite immigration policy, to be paid to a certain colonization company which has been more or less discredited in the country. But we, the people of Canada, who are indirectly to pay that $500,000 are to have no voice in the matter whatever. The situation is simply intolerable.
Now, I am not going to criticize Sir Henry Thornton concerning the many speeches he has made throughout the country. But I would point out that whilst the reason for having an independent board is essentially that the railways should be kept out of politics, there is a very real danger that Sir Henry Thornton may assume, in the political life of the country,, a position that is not accorded to any man elected to represent the people on the floor of this House. Sir Henry Thornton can go about the country advocating immigration and whatever else he likes, and he says he is doing it for business reasons. But these policies which he is advocating may be essentially public policies. Sir Henry Thomton is not responsible for these utterances to any group of people in this country. I suppose he is here on a contract for a term of years; but he is not subject to the scrutiny that is exercised over one of the ministers of the Crown. Again I say that we are allowing things to drift into a very serious situation if we permit an organization to grow up which is not at all responsible to the people of the country.
A similar situation prevails in connection with the shipping corporations throughout the country. Our merchant marine has become part of the railway system or at least is connected with it. We are allowing our president of this great railway company to act on shipping boards and possibly join with our other corporations that are keeping up freight rates, and having no small share in determining the commercial and financial policies of the people.
I	submit that these are powers that should not be granted to any one man. I know that under the rules and regulations of this House we are comparatively helpless. Apparently
about the only thing we can do is

carry these estimates and not give any information; it can invest in real estate in Paris this year or, if it chooses, in Berlin next year; it can invest in real estate in various countries of the world with which our railways may have some connection. Now to-night this matter comes before us in what strikes me as a most extraordinary way. There is not a point on which the minister dare commit himself definitely, and what information he does possess he is unable to reveal. Yet he is actually asking for a large sum of money. Now, we all appreciate the immense difficulty of running this railway system as a public enterprise and at the same time giving detailed information to parliament and to the country in advance of the completion of various transactions. That is something that obviously cannot be done unless we are to pay through the nose time and again for what we want, and I do not wish any word of mine to interfere with any reasonable policy which will avoid that. But there is a body that lies between the management of the Canadian National Railways and the general public, a body that I think ought to be informed as to all the essential parts of every such transaction. That body is the government of Canada, which, whether we support it or not, has been chosen by the people to be their stewards until they make a change. Now, if we are going to set

up a power in Canada that will be greater than the government, that will have its secrets from the government, and to which the government must go with bated breath truckling. for a little necessary information, then I say something is growing up too big for Canada itself. The minister apparently had not been entrusted with knowledge of this project before an irrevocable step was taken by the head of the railway system. Do not think, Mr. Chairman, that I purpose to-night to abuse or even to criticize Sir Henry Thornton. I do not think the time has come for that. He ought at least to be consulted; he ought at least to have an opportunity of laying the matter before his colleagues. If that is not done, responsible government becomes very largely a farce. Most of the time we spend in this parliament is devoted to criticism of estimates, the voting of supply, and very often on trivial, minor matters hours and days of the time of this House are taken up; yet when we come to a matter of this magnitude we are expected to pass it through, even with a confession from the government itself that it does not know the details of the transaction. been able to have faith in the wisdom of public ownership and public administration of a railway system, and I have not got it now. The very existence of such circumstances as we are discussing to-night is enough, I think, to revolt the strongest advocate of public ownership from the doctrine that he has been prone to profess. When I am told that it is within the four corners of the act that the president of the railway may make a bargain behind the back of the government and of the people of Canada, then I say that a system which, [DOT]even though it may be technically lawful, permits a total disregard of the opinion of the people themselves and of the government of 'Canada $s not a system that in the end will produce beneficial results. You may for r time under exceptional men and in exceptional circumstances- get some benefit, but you will not in the long run. I will be asked, perhaps, what stand my party is taking in this matter.
That is important.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks of the last speaker (Mr. Baxter) lead me to think that it might be advisable to get a farmer on that railway board so that things might be properly managed. I have listened very patiently to-night to a great deal of eloquence to see if we could .get some information in connection with this veiy mysterious deal that has taken place over in Paris. I am inclined to think, Mr. Chairman, that something has got out a little too early and that that is all there is to it. I do not think the trouble with the minister is lack of knowledge; no doubt he has information that perhaps it may not be exactly to the public interest to disclose. It is rather unfortunate that such a thing should happen; perhaps it would have been better had this discussion not taken place before completion of the transaction and the laying of the information on the Table of the House so that we should know all about it.
I do not like some of the criticisms that have been levelled at Sir Henry Thornton. He has undertaken a great work, and I think perhaps it would help him to feel that he has the confidence of the public. There is something in human nature that makes a man generally try to live up to his reputation, [DOT] and the very fact that we expect him to do well, that he knows we place our confidence in him will be an incentive to him to. go on and make a success of the Canadian National railway. I believe it is going to be a success.
I make a guess that next year if we have reasonable crops in the West we will have four or five times the surplus over operating expenses that we had this year. I am not a prophet nor perhaps a great business expert, but I have that faith in the management and the way things are shaping at the present time.
In connection with the renting of what we may call expensive buildings in some of the principal cities where traffic might originate,

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
although I am in favour of economy I believe that a great institution like the Canadian National railway cannot afford to have a shabby place in any of these great centres.
What about Toronto?

Take the city of Toronto. Would you like to see the Canadian National Railways, office there located on some back street, or on the back street in any other great city? I would be even more ambitious than that yet.
There is another question that looms up in my mind. It has been before the House, and it is perhaps looking a little too far ahead, but this is perhaps a good time to mention it. We have been trying to work up a trade in exporting cattle to Great Britain. I am going to express the opinion that just so long as we trust to the shipping companies to export our cattle the trade will not be a very great success, because the shipping companies are so few and they amalgamate so easily that I believe the rates will be fixed at such a point that only a few cattle will cross and perhaps the trade will be killed altogether. I think the day is not far distant when it may be necessary to take the merchant marine out into real deep water and sink them. I believe it will be possible in the not distant future for the Canadian National Railways to have a line of steamships just as the Canadian Pacific has to-day.
Proper steamships.

Proper steamships that will carry cattle. I would not say go into the business of having any big steamship line, but they could rent or build just sufficient to demonstrate to the people of this country at what rate cattle could be carried across the ocean at a profitable figure. Otherwise I do not believe the trade of shipping cattle to the Old Country will ever amount to anything. That may seem rather ambitious to suggest of an organization that has a large deficit every year, but I believe in having courage and 1 believe this is a time for courage. The only way we can make the railways pay is by making them a going concern with ocean traffic and business offices everywhere where trade could originate.
Coming back to the commencement of my remarks I would be rather sorry for the Minister of Railways were he not built exactly as he is, but I see that he is standing up fairly well under the ordeal. I know there is a suspicious look about this $2,000,000 transaction about which we can get no information, but I am inclined to think that the real trouble is that it has got on the boards a little too early and the minister cannot divulge all he knows. We will simply have to preserve our souls in patience and make up our minds that the government is going to get in great trouble when we get the facts if everything is not all right.

I was pleased
to hear the minister make the statement that the rents from the Yonge street building recently acquired will cover the investment. I was going to ask the minister, does he hope to carry this item to-night?
Yes.

What is his
idea-that the committee sit till what hour?
Four o'clock.

I am not trying to bulldoze the committee at all. I had hoped to get this item through to-night. I was going to take up the merchant marine, but the leader of the Opposition was going away and asked me to keep some railway item, which I intended to do, on which he could discuss the subject. This is an item of some magnitude, and I thought perhaps we could get it through to-night and reserve some other item on which there could be a general discussion.

If my hon.
friend did that he would, I think, be doing something that never has been done in this House before. This is the main item on which the great bulk of the discussions necessarily takes place. There are a great many other items that could have been brought on. We have all the items, for instance, from 116 to 122 inclusive, and then we have the items from 123 to 140 with some omissions.
Some are through.
I do not think my hon. friend had any vety great hopes than the item would go through to-night.
Yes I had.
I can tell him it will not. We can put in the time just as well as he can.
My hon. friend is talking as if I had made a threat. He must be bad natured to-night.

The Minister
of Marine and Fisheries said four o'clock, and I did not hear any contradiction from my genial frieh'd. "
Supply-Railwa ys-C .N.R.

We are trying to make
some progress. If we are going to get through any time this summer we shall have to work a little later than we have been doing. But I am not trying to force the committee to do anything.

Why not bring on any
one of these dozen smaller items? We could have passed a string of them. There are fifteen items here more or less unimportant, but this is the $73,000,000 item.

They are all important,
but I am not going to quarrel with my hon. friend.

My hon. friend cannot
quarrel with me.
My hon. friend from West York said that this item had never been put through before so quickly. It was put through in thirty mitutes last year.

Last year we were told that the government did not know anything about the business. We agreed. We were very sympathetic. We gave them no trouble at all. But now they are supposed to know something about it and we are finding out things we never knew anything about before.

I would point out that last year they were my hon. friend's own estimates, or practically his own, and he had such confidence in them that he did not wish to have any light thrown on them, and so did not ask any questions. I think we might discuss this item a little longer to see if there is any further information that my hon friends want and then we could go on with some of the other items.
If we are going on with anything else I think we should go on with it now. We sat last night till three o'clock.
Do not blame me for that.
I do not know. I think we should blame the government for it altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Blame it
for everything.
I should like to know whether we are going on with this item or going to take up some of the other items, or whether we are going to adjourn.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There are other members to speak on this vote.
fSir Henry Drayton.]
Does the government desire that we should go on with this vote to-night?
Go on for a little while, it is only 11.30.
Why not let this stand and call some other item?
I am not objecting to that, but we want to make some progress, that i.s all.

I think you
would make progress by taking up another item. I would like definitely to know what the government's idea is? My view is that we will make more progress by letting this item stand. The minister will find he will make more progress by letting this item stand.
That is a threat.

No, it is not a threat. It is a mere statement of fact because we might get some information in the meantime from the minister. For example, the minister might wish to bring down the extract from the minutes of the meeting of the directors. We might even find out whether the matter had even gone as far as that. If I remember rightly the minister told us that he could not say that anybody knew anything about it except the president and the solicitor; he did not know that it had come before the board even. Perhaps we could find out about that. Then I had a very disquieting statement made to me to-day with reference to Toronto. Perhaps we could find out if that is true or not. That statement is to this effect: That the company were buying not only the comer of King and Yonge streets but they were also buying the Home bank and had already been committed to that purchase. I do not know whether there is a word of truth in this statement or not but I would like the minister to find out.
I can tell my hon. friend now.
That there is not a word of truth in it?
My hon. friend would find it a great deal easier to make progress if this matter had been done legally and properly.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: What about the rumours?
If the action taken had been legal and proper my hon. friend's position would not be nearly so difficult.
I am speaking about the situation in Toronto.
I am referring to the Paris matter.

My hon. friend asked me a question about Toronto and said he had heard disquieting rumours about what had been done there. That statement goes on Hansard and is circulated throughout the country, and there is not one word of truth in it.	.

Nevertheless I am still going to ask my hon. friend to look into the matter. I am going to ask him to find out whether an offer was not made to the bank directorate, and whether a bank director was not engaged in negotiations. It may be that there is nothing in the rumour; but when we find that the country can be committed to a $2,000,000 proposition without the slightest notice or warning it is just as well to find out if there is anything in it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: You have got a suspicious mind.
Now then I assume-
It pays to advertise.
I assume I may thank my hon. friend for his kind remark.
Hear, hear.
It is a splendid advertisement. I do not know that I can improve the model my hon. friend has set up.
Oh no, you are better at that yourself.

It would be a task entirely beyond me. Nevertheless I thank my hon. friend for his admonition. Now, Mr. Chairman, I suppose we can take it for granted that the minister is not going to tell us anything more about the Paris purchase. Can he tell us, though, whether the deed has yet been taken for that property, whether the two millions has yet been paid to the original owner?

I am not sure about that.
I am informed it has been done through the London office.
So the money is gone and we have the property.
No.
My hon. friend says no. We cannot eat our cake and have it. If the money has been paid it must be gone.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: You do not want the company to have any property in Paris?
Can the minister tell me from whom the property was purchased?
From the owners.
I suppose it would be the company. I do not know the name of the company.
You could not tell us as to that? Is that the whole price? Was everything paid in cash?
A little under $2,000,000.

Was it all paid in cash? I see. So there is no balance left at all. Well, Mr. Chairman, if the minister will not tell us anything about it I shall not tell him what attitude we will take in connection with it. I want full particulars of item (a) "Operating deficits whenever incurred or ascertained." What is the amount put in under that item?

My hon. friend has a perfect right to this information. I do not like his threats, though.
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
There are no threats.	.

There were absolute
threats, but we cannot do business in that way. You cannot make any headway and we cannot do any business.
I offered to take some other item.

You did not give me a chance to accept, you kept on talking instead of sitting down. The operating deficit for the Canadian Government Railways themselves-I think we are providing liberally for these but we have to make provision for all eventualities-is $3,000,000; for the Canadian Northern, $2,500,000; for the Grand Trunk Railway nothing; for the Grand Trunk Pacific $4,500,000, totalling $10,000,000.

Before we leave this vote there is a condition to which I would like to draw attention in connection with the St. John and Quebec railway which the Dominion government is operating at the present time. As you possibly know we had floods in New Brunswick this spring. In April a bridge was washed away on the St. John and Quebec railway just above Woodstock. There were several washouts on the Canadian Pacific railway which runs up through nearly the same territory, at the same time. The Canadian Pacific Railway Com-pan}', however, were able to restore their service within a week anyway. The Canadian National railway bridge is still down. I understand there was a lapse of thirty days from the time the bridge went out before operations were begun to replace it. The latest information I have is that they expect it will be the first of July before' they will have that road in operation.
Where is the bridge to which you refer?
I will bring the remarks of my hon. friend to the attention of the management to-morrow.

Perhaps the minister can give me an answer now in reference to the train shed at St. John. Does he know whether the president or board of directors or somebody has arranged for the building of a new station there?
No, it is not provided for in this estimate, I am afraid.

Is there any provision for renewing the bridge at Fredericton? The minister may not know, but that bridge was built in 1887 by the late Senator Temple, and it is now considered too light for the class of locomotives that have to go over it, with the result that all the trains passing over that now have to be hauled by small engines. Large engines cannot go over the bridge across the river. The matter has been under consideration, and we have been waiting for more than three years. Could the minister Bay whether a new bridge is contemplated there?
There is no provision in the estimates for that.
If the minister does not want us to continue with this general item, I will not press it now. I can ask the question again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This is a general item, 139 under which all those items may be discussed.

Will that new station be dealt with in Lhe Supplementary Estimates,
Supply-Railways and Canals

or has the railway board decided that during the coming year nothing will be done? Will it be built out of revenue or will anything be done?

No doubt in the world the board recognizes the urgency or necessity, but in regard to much of this work we have to make selections, and I am told that they are going to impose on the people of St. John for another year. They have not put anything in the estimates for that station.

Does the minister realize what it means, not only to the people of St. John, who, of course, use the railway station to some extent, or rather who suffer for the want of a railway station, but to the whole passenger traffic coming from St. John? It means people have to get on or off the train in what was a train-shed, but what is now simply out of doors, in all kinds of weather. Such a condition does not exist in any city or town, I think, of one-quarter the size of St. John throughout the Dominion of Canada, and it is even more disgraceful than the filthy station that people have to put up with in the city of Toronto, when there is a good station alongside; and I must say I do not know why it is not being used.
Item stands.
To provide for the purchase of branch lines-
Moncton and Buctouche Railway-
Revote	 $70,000
Interest estimated, from date of taking possession to March 31, 1924, not exceeding (including Revote-$21,125)..	..	23,625
This is an old item that has been voted year after year. The railways have not been able to get title to the property.

I want to tell the minister that if the company will get down to brass tacks and pay their liabilities they will get the title to the right-of-way. Under the provincial legislation they do not own the right-of-way. This railway company never had title to the right-of-way, by deed or grant of any kind. Enabling legislation was passed by the provincial government providing that on certain proof being submitted to the Lieutenant Governor in Council a vesting order should be passed. This road is head over heels in debt to legitimate creditors, but it has absolutely refused to make any effort to pay them, with the result that the provincial government of New Brunswick, very properly, and at the instance of residents of the province to whom the company is indebted, has refused to make this vesting order. The minister will never

get title to the right-of-way until he obtains that vesting order, and that order will not be got until he brings pressure to bear upon the management of the Moncton and Buctouche railway to pay their creditors. I can frankly say that I am interested in one of these claims for an estate which has been waiting patiently for a long time to get the money that is due it. We do not seem to be able to make any progress in the matter, and I would ask the minister, as in days gone by I have asked the deputy minister, to interest himself and to tell these people to clean up their liabilities so that these claimants may be able to get their money. There will be very little coming to the owners of the road and the matter should be attended to.

Item agreed to.
To pay claim of Fortin & Moffatt (National Transcontinental Railway), $5,390.

This is an old claim. Settlement was agreed to by the late Mr. Cochrane, but at that time the men would not take the amount offered. They have visited me once or twice and I have informed them that I am prepared to give them this amount in settlement of the claim of $29,000. If they do not accept this in full they will get nothing.

Item agreed to.
St. Anne's lock: highway bridge at Isle Perrot, $100,000.

This is a grant for a
bridge, part of which has been paid.

I do not want to say
much, but is this bridge more important than some cover for the people who are using trains in the city of St. John?
Where is the bridge?
At Isle Perrot.
Where is that?

My hon. friend behind
me (Mr. Lavigueur) can inform the hon. gentleman. This is for the construction of a bridge between the island and the mainland. The federal government has made a contribution, part of which has been paid.

Before the item is
carried I want to make one or two observations. I see that the government is subscribing $400,000 for the construction of a bridge at Isle Perrot. I may point out that a bridge is projected on the island of Orleans, Quebec, and we shall look to the government for a contribution to that undertaking. I think the provincial government of Quebec

Supply-Canals
is well disposed to build a bridge which will cost probably about $800,000, or, say, a million, to provide communication with the mainland for a population of six very important agricultural parishes on the island of Orleans. I have no objection to this item being passed, but I wish to have it understood now that at the next session of parliament I shall call upon the government for a subscription towards the construction of that bridge.

I am not objecting to the item, but I want to know on what principle the government could contribute to a bridge wholly within the province of Quebec. If they adopted that principle I am sure they would be invited to contribute to many other similar undertakings. I am plead-
12 m. ing at present with the Minister of Public Works for a contribution towards an international bridge which is of great importance to the country from the standpoint of international obligations. Only a modest sum of $17,500 is involved, and I hope to see provision for it in the Estimates, so that our friends in the state of Maine will not be able to regard us as pikers. This particular bridge, I understand, is wholly within the province of Quebec.
Which one?
This one.

Do I understand that the hon. member is referring to the bridge between Vaudreuil and Isle Perrot? So far as I know, this is being built by subsidy from the provincial government and by federal subscription. Is the bridge which the hon. gentleman refers to a construction under the highways grant?
No, this is a special vote.

If my hon. friend will allow me I will inform him. The federal
government is assisting to build the bridge over its own canal.

Item agreed to.
St. Lawrence ship canal-surveys and investigations, $50,000.
What is being done there?
This work has been carried on continuously. The time will come when the data from these surveys will be essential. The work is done without any great blare of trumpets, but thoroughly, nevertheless.

Item agreed to.
Hudson Bay Railway-Port Nelson terminals, $40,000.
This is for the care of the terminals already constructed.
Will provision be made to meet the undertaking given to the House some time ago in regard to bringing the line into a proper state of repair? Will that be provided for?
Before Christmas?
The minister cannot make . any provision. He can make suggestions to his colleagues who can submit recommendations to parliament. I had in mind asking for an appropriation for that purpose.
Are we to understand that the minister has made up his mind to ask his colleagues for that appropriation? May we have his assurance to that effect?

As a member of the
government I do not like to make definite pledges, but I will do like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), I will ask my hon. friend to "wait and see." I think he will not be disappointed.

Item agreed to.
Trent canal improvements, $255,000.
What returns are we receiving from this canal?

I would not suggest that we get any straight returns. The only return is in the development of one of the most beautiful sections of Ontario. If my hon. friend ever wants to take a trip for his health I would recommend him to go along the Trent Valley canal which will take him through a very beautiful country and he will find hospitality, all along the route.
But it is of no practical utility.
I would not say so. I think a tourist traffic can be developed there as well as a traffic for light draft freight boats We do get a return in the shape of rent for power development.
My recollection is that this is merely maintenance work.
Yes, dams and that sort of thing.

We have been voting very large sums of money annually for this canal, and I was wondering if there was any traffic to warrant the building of the locks and the continuance of this heavy expenditure.

Supply-Railways
We are living in hopes that; there will be greater traffic. But if we do not maintain the works great flood damage will result.
Is the Atherley bridge appropriation in this item?
Yes.

Is there any chance to get the minister to do what the deputation, representatives I think of all parties in this House, impressed upon him, namely, to take over this bridge, the counties concerned contributing $15,000 each. With the $25,000 contribution from the government there is only another $2,000 or $3,000 required to meet the total cost of the bridge, $58,000. Cannot the minister see his way clear to go this little extra distance? This bridge is over the canal system, and I think the request is reasonable. Many other bridges on the canal have been taken over. There is no politics in this proposal, and it is an absolutely fair one. As a last effort I would suggest that the minister make up the extra $2,000 or $3,000. Even if the counties were called upon to make a little more generous contribution I think they might be inclined to do so if the minister will take the bridge over.

I have discussed it with my officials, and I am advised that the taking over of the bridges along the Trent canal is becoming such a problem that I hesitate to go as far as I am requested in regard to this bridge. However, I will discuss it again with the officials. The time will probably come when we will take over most of the bridges, but I should not like to hold out too much hope at the present time.
I thought the minister might go the extra distance. I think it has been done in other cases.
We will look into the matter.

The bridge should be constructed without delay, and if the department is going to take in hand the construction under departmental specifications, it might as well take the bridge over. On the other hand, if the department is only going to make a contribution, that is a different proposition, and the difficulty is if it is to be further looked into the construction of the bridge will be held up for another year. If I thought for one minute the minister would seriously look into it further I would be glad to get the members from the other ridings together-they represent all parties in this House-and have them spend a few minutes with him. I feel the claim is so

absolutely righteous and fair that it ought to be allowed, and I so addressed myself to the minister when we saw him. Indeed, I thought we had impressed him and that he would accede to our request.
I almost yielded.

I think you did at the time, and it was the suavity the minister is so famous for which accounted for the absence of further discussion. If the minister will reconsider it I would ask him to let this item stand.
You had better let it go through, otherwise there will be no appropriation.
Then there is still hope?
We will look further into the matter.

Item agreed to.
Surveys and Inspections, Railways: including salaries and expenses of experts employed temporarily, $55,000.
Are there any surveys for new branch lines?
This is rather departmental. We have a lot of that special work and send men out to do it.
Is there any large survey in contemplation for branch lines anywhere?
If there be any surveys they will be rather under a vote for that special purpose.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Fielding the House adjourned at 12.10 a.m. (Friday).
